Chapter 9

Collaborative Technical Practices and Decision Making

协作性技术实践与决策制定

In chaotic environments, the difference between success and failure often hinges on how effectively teams work together and make technical decisions. Without robust collaborative practices, even the most talented engineers can build the wrong things, creating unnecessary complexity or duplicating efforts—not to mention the inherent friction, discord, and conflict created by confusion and misdirection. For you to succeed, decision making needs to be crisp and fast, and everyone needs to move in the same direction quickly and safely.

在混乱的环境中，成功与失败的区别往往取决于团队能否高效协作并做出技术决策。没有扎实的协作实践，即便是最有天赋的工程师也可能造出错误的东西，制造不必要的复杂性或重复劳动——更不用说困惑与错误导向本身就会带来摩擦、不和与冲突。要想成功，决策必须干脆而迅速，每个人都必须快速、安全地朝同一个方向前进。

Chaotic environments are already stressful, and if your team (and your leadership style) isn’t in routine or doesn’t support you, then working at a chaotic organization goes from being potentially stressful to untenable. In this chapter, we explore how to establish effective collaborative technical practices and decision-making frameworks that can thrive even in the most chaotic and turbulent organizations.

混乱的环境本就充满压力；如果你的团队（以及你的领导风格）没有形成常态、或不给你支持，那么在一家混乱的组织里工作就会从“可能有压力”变成“难以忍受”。本章我们探讨如何建立有效的协作技术实践与决策框架，使之即便在最混乱、最动荡的组织中也能蓬勃生长。

In Chapter 6, we discussed the dangers of processes for their own sake and the tendency of extensive, unwieldy processes that lead to inertia and inefficiency. We talked about being agile, starting with the smallest amount of process and then building on that, only if needed. The same advice applies to building collaboration and leveling up decision making. In our experience, people innovate in light-touch environments and they stagnate in high-touch environments.

在第 6 章里，我们讨论了“为流程而流程”的危险，以及臃肿、笨拙的流程如何导致惰性与低效。我们谈到要敏捷——从最少的流程起步，只在确有需要时才往上加。同样的建议也适用于搭建协作、提升决策水平。以我们的经验，人在轻触（light-touch）环境中会创新，在高触（high-touch）环境中会停滞。

We also introduced the concept of (shared) technical principles in Chapter 8. These will lead out this chapter, too. Like technical architecture, they make a good foundation for building good technical practices and making good decisions.

我们在第 8 章还引入了（共享的）技术原则这一概念。它们也将贯穿本章。和技术架构一样，它们为建立良好的技术实践、做出良好的决策打下了好地基。

Shared Technical Principles

共享技术原则

As we discussed in Chapter 8, technical principles serve as the foundation for engineering decisions, guiding both strategic planning and daily implementation. These principles aren’t meant to be rigid rules but rather guides that help teams navigate complex technical landscapes. When developed collaboratively, they create a shared understanding of what “good” looks like in your organization, and they provide a framework for consistent decision making across teams and projects.

正如第 8 章所讨论的，技术原则是工程决策的基石，同时指导战略规划与日常实现。这些原则不是死板的规则，而是帮助团队在复杂技术版图中航行的指南。当它们由团队共同制定时，会在组织内形成对“好是什么样子”的共同理解，并为跨团队、跨项目的一致决策提供框架。

Also in Chapter 8, we articulated 14 proposed principles:

同样在第 8 章，我们给出了 14 条拟定原则：

  • Simplicity first

    简洁优先

  • Visibility

    可见性

  • Scalability

    可扩展性

  • Security by design

    设计期安全（Security by design）

  • Modularity

    模块化

  • Performance awareness

    性能意识

  • Reliability

    可靠性

  • Consistency

    一致性

  • Maintainability

    可维护性

  • Automation

    自动化

  • Documentation

    文档

  • Openness

    开放性

  • Testing

    测试

  • Evolution

    演进性

Importantly, for this chapter, you’ll notice that almost none of the example technical principles can be interpreted as purely technical. Sure, most of them have a technical aspect, but they also include social or cultural elements; this isn’t by accident.

对本章而言，有一点很重要：你会注意到，这些示例技术原则几乎没有一条能被解读为纯粹技术性的。当然，它们大多有技术的一面，但也包含社会或文化的成分；这并非偶然。

Some of this is natural; principles tend to be more abstract than concepts like linting rules. You might build linting rules based on a technical principle. Still, it doesn’t make much sense to specify tabs or spaces as a technical principle because of two main reasons:

其中一部分是自然的：原则往往比 lint 规则这类概念更抽象。你可以基于某条技术原则去制定 lint 规则。但把“用 Tab 还是空格”规定为一条技术原则就没多大意义，主要原因有二：

  • It’s a very narrow focus.

    它的关注点太窄。

  • It doesn’t deliver any real value to the team.

    它不会给团队带来任何真正的价值。

If you were to take that approach, your technical principles become overly detailed, and could start resembling a government paper:

如果你真这么干，技术原则就会变得过于琐碎，开始像一份政府公文：

…section A, subsection 4, paragraph 7, clause 8, line 16 deals with the use of spaces (see section G.1.1.2 for definitions of “spaces” and space volumes) versus tabs (see section G.1.1.2 for definitions of “tab” as a spatial construct)…

…A 节第 4 小节第 7 段第 8 条第 16 行，论及空格的使用（“空格”及空格体量的定义见 G.1.1.2 节）与 Tab 的对比（作为空间构造物的“Tab”定义见 G.1.1.2 节）…

— 原书第 194 页 —

And then they become impossible to reason about and, frankly, hinder innovation. Other aspects are more deliberate consequences of articulating principles that focus on the intersection of people and technology. You see, technical principles do double duty: they guide technical implementation and shape your team’s culture and social dynamics.

那样的东西根本没法拿来推理，坦白说还会阻碍创新。另一部分则是有意为之的结果——把原则聚焦在人与技术的交汇处来表述。你看，技术原则是身兼二职的：它既指导技术实现，也塑造团队的文化与社交生态。

Take “simplicity first,” for example. On the surface, this principle is about writing cleaner code with fewer moving parts. But in practice, it transforms how your team operates on a day-to-day basis. When an engineer starts suggesting an elaborate, 12-microservice solution to a problem that could be solved with a simple API endpoint, “simplicity first” gives the team permission to pump the brakes and ask, “Do we need all that complexity?”

以“简洁优先”为例。表面上，这条原则讲的是写出更干净、活动部件更少的代码。但在实践中，它会改变团队日常运作的方式。当一位工程师对一个本可用简单 API 端点解决的问题，提出一套精巧的、12 个微服务的方案时，“简洁优先”就给了团队踩刹车的许可，让他们敢问一句：“我们真需要这么复杂吗？”

“Simplicity first” also doesn’t just become a default response to scope creep. In planning meetings, when requirements start ballooning, the team can say, “Let’s simplify first,” and refocus on the essential problem. This principle then shapes not just architecture but the entire approach to work—from how you run meetings (shorter, more focused) to how you onboard new team members—starting with core concepts before diving into details.

“简洁优先”也不仅仅是应对需求蔓延的默认反应。在规划会议上，当需求开始膨胀时，团队可以说“我们先把它简化”，重新聚焦到本质问题上。这条原则于是不仅塑造架构，还塑造整个工作方式——从你怎么开会（更短、更聚焦），到你怎么带新人入职——先从核心概念讲起，再深入细节。

Or consider the principle of “documentation.” Beyond ensuring your code has comments, this principle cultivates knowledge-sharing behaviors. Teams that value documentation tend to develop cultures where teaching others is celebrated. They’re more collaborative because they understand that undocumented knowledge creates dangerous dependencies on specific individuals.

再看“文档”这条原则。它不只确保你的代码有注释，更培养了知识分享的行为习惯。重视文档的团队往往会发展出一种“教别人是值得庆祝的事”的文化。他们更协作，因为他们明白：没写下来的知识会造成对特定个人的危险依赖。

The beauty of technical principles is that they create a shared language that bridges technical implementation and human behavior. When your team invokes the “automation” principle, they’re not just talking about writing infrastructure as code; they’re reinforcing a culture that values everyone’s time and focuses human energy on creative problem-solving rather than repetitive tasks.

技术原则的美妙之处在于：它们创造了一种共同语言，把技术实现与人的行为桥接起来。当团队援引“自动化”原则时，他们不只是在谈把基础设施写成代码；他们是在强化一种文化——珍视每个人的时间，把人的精力集中到创造性的问题解决上，而不是重复性的琐事上。

These principles should become cultural touchstones, invoked in meetings and Slack threads. They help new team members understand how things are done far more effectively than any employee handbook. They’re powerful precisely because they operate at the intersection of technology and people, guiding both what you build and how you work together to build it.

这些原则应当成为文化试金石，在会议和 Slack 话题里被反复援引。它们帮助新人理解“事情是怎么做成的”，效果远胜任何员工手册。它们之所以有力，正是因为它们运作在技术与人的交汇处，既指导你造什么，也指导你如何协作去造。

In Practice: April’s Story

实践案例：April 的故事

At PixelCurl, April saw this principle–culture connection firsthand. When she arrived, there were no shared principles—just three different philosophies from three senior engineers. Marcus believed in “performance above all,” optimizing every millisecond even if it meant unreadable code. Sarah championed “move fast and break things,” shipping features quickly but leaving a trail of bugs. Derek practiced “fortress engineering,” building bulletproof systems that took months to modify. But this resulted in junior engineers getting whiplash trying to follow three contradictory approaches. So, April facilitated a principles workshop where they arrived at their first shared principle: “simplicity first.” Within weeks, code reviews became less combative. Marcus stopped writing incomprehensible one-liners that saved 2 ms but cost hours to debug, Sarah started adding error handling instead of assuming happy paths, and Derek began accepting “good enough” solutions that could ship in the correct quarter instead of the next year.

在 PixelCurl，April 亲眼见证了这种“原则—文化”关联。她刚到任时，团队没有共享原则，只有三位资深工程师各自奉行的三套哲学。Marcus 信奉“性能高于一切”，哪怕代码变得不可读也要优化每一毫秒；Sarah 鼓吹“快速行动、打破陈规”，飞快地发功能，身后留下一串bug；Derek 则搞“堡垒工程”，造出刀枪不入、却要改好几个月的系统。结果初级工程师们被三套互相矛盾的做法晃得晕头转向。于是 April 主持了一场原则工作坊，大家定下了第一条共享原则：“简洁优先”。几周之内，代码评审不再剑拔弩张。Marcus 不再写那种能省 2 毫秒、却要花几小时调试的天书般单行代码；Sarah 开始补错误处理，而不是默认一切顺利；Derek 也开始接受“足够好”、能在本季度（而非明年）交付的方案。

Making Technical Principles Stick

让技术原则真正落地

Making technical principles stick requires visibility and regular reinforcement. Rather than tucking them away in a forgotten document or slide deck, you and your team (and this is ideal work for staff and principal engineers to wield influence) need to prominently display principles and reference them regularly during design discussions, code reviews, and planning sessions. We’ve seen organizations that printed their technical principles on the wall of their main workspace. For James, who is somewhat of a cynic, it initially seemed theatrical. Still, he’s come to appreciate that there is a power in having principles be a natural part of vocabulary.

要让技术原则真正落地，需要可见度和反复强化。别把它们塞进一份被遗忘的文档或幻灯片里——你和你的团队（这恰恰是 staff / principal 级工程师发挥影响力的理想抓手）需要把原则醒目地展示出来，并在设计讨论、代码评审和规划会议中经常援引。我们见过有公司把技术原则打印出来贴在主办公区的墙上。对多少有点愤世嫉俗的 James 来说，起初这显得很做作。但他逐渐体会到：让原则成为日常词汇的一部分，本身就有一种力量。

Mission statements, vision statements, and technical principles only become items without power if they are treated as props or parroted as rhetoric. If they are treated with respect and reinforced, then they become touchstones that push people to do better. In chaotic environments, we’ve learned that morale, team unity, and focus are fragile things; cultural touchpoints like this reinforce that unity and continuity.

使命宣言、愿景宣言和技术原则，只有被当成摆设、被当成口号鹦鹉学舌时，才会变成没有力量的东西。如果它们被认真对待、被反复强化，就会成为推动人们做得更好的试金石。在混乱的环境里，我们认识到士气、团队凝聚力和专注力都是脆弱的东西；这样的文化锚点会强化这种团结与延续。

Perhaps even more important than displaying principles is modeling them through leadership behavior. If you preach simplicity but approve overly complex designs, or champion documentation while leaving your code undocumented, your team will follow your actions, not your words. The disconnect between stated principles and leadership behavior creates cynicism and undermines the entire framework. Technical leaders must demonstrate their commitment to these principles through their work and decisions, creating a culture where principles are lived rather than just spoken.

也许比展示原则更重要的，是通过领导行为去示范它们。如果你口口声声讲简洁，却批准过于复杂的设计；如果你鼓吹文档，自己的代码却不留文档——团队会仿效你的行动，而不是你的言辞。宣称的原则与领导行为之间的脱节会滋生犬儒心态，并瓦解整个框架。技术领导者必须通过自己的工作和决策来证明对这些原则的承诺，营造一种原则被“活出来”而非只被“说出来”的文化。

Technical principles should evolve as your organization changes. Schedule regular reviews, perhaps quarterly, to assess whether your principles still align with your team’s goals and challenges. This keeps them relevant and reinforces their

技术原则应当随组织的变化而演进。安排定期评审（比如每季度一次），检视原则是否仍与团队的目标和挑战对齐。这能让它们保持时效性，并强化它们的

— 原书第 196 页 —

importance. The review process itself can be a valuable opportunity for team discussion, helping newer team members understand the rationale behind each principle and enabling everyone to contribute to their refinement. As your team grows and technology evolves, your principles may need to adapt while still preserving their core intent.

重要性。评审过程本身也是宝贵的团队讨论契机：帮助新人理解每条原则背后的理由，并让每个人都能参与原则的打磨。随着团队成长、技术演进，你的原则可能需要调整，但仍要保留其核心意图。

Communication, Collaboration, and Execution

沟通、协作与执行

Effective communication is essential for collaboration, yet teams frequently face obstacles in this area. Nowhere is this more obvious than in shipping products. Imagine your team’s product (and its requirements, codebase, and execution) as a shared kitchen where everyone’s cooking different dishes simultaneously. When engineers are all working in the same space without talking to each other, then it’s hard to reason about what to cook, how many ingredients you need, and where your kitchen utensils are. This kind of uncoordinated effort leads to confusion, duplicate work, and sometimes even a few burnt meals.

有效的沟通是协作的前提，但团队在这方面屡屡碰壁。这一点在交付产品时体现得最为明显。把你团队的产品（以及它的需求、代码库和执行）想象成一个共用厨房，大家同时在做不同的菜。当工程师们都在同一个空间里干活却互不交谈时，你就很难想清楚要做什么菜、需要多少食材、厨具都放在哪儿。这种各自为政的忙活会导致混乱、重复劳动，有时还会炒糊几盘菜。

So, how do you solve this? The most common natural reaction is to enforce collaboration and communication through rigid structure and centralized command and control. We can extend our kitchen metaphor to provide an exploration of why this doesn’t work. Professional kitchens rely on the brigade system. In this well-defined structure, everyone has their station and clear responsibilities. The head chef (tech lead) coordinates the overall vision, while station chefs (senior engineers) oversee specific areas, such as sauces, meats, or desserts (databases, frontend, APIs). Less experienced chefs work within these stations, learning the craft while staying in their assigned area. The magic allegedly happens because everyone knows exactly where their responsibilities begin and end, communication follows established patterns (“Yes, chef!”), and the implication is that the structure allows for both specialization and smooth coordination.

那怎么解决呢？最常见的本能反应是：用死板的结构和集中式的命令与控制来强制协作和沟通。我们把厨房的比喻再延伸一下，来看看为什么这招不灵。专业后厨靠的是“厨师团队制”（brigade system）。在这套界定清晰的结构里，每个人有自己的岗位和明确职责。主厨（技术负责人）统筹整体愿景，各岗位厨师（资深工程师）分管特定领域，比如酱汁、肉类或甜点（对应数据库、前端、API）。经验较浅的厨师在这些岗位内干活，待在自己被分配的区域里学艺。据说魔法就这么发生了：每个人都清楚自己的职责从哪开始、到哪结束，沟通遵循既定模式（“是，主厨！”），言下之意是这种结构既允许专业化，又能顺畅协作。

Ah, no. Both James and Juan worked in the hospitality industry. Indeed, Juan was a professional chef before turning to the dark side, and the brigade system is a good example of how not to collaborate to ship products. The strict hierarchies and rigid role definitions of the brigade system often fail when building products. The brigade system was designed for execution and repetition, not creation. A restaurant kitchen’s primary goal is to repeatedly produce the same dishes to specification, night after night. The head chef designs the menu, and everyone else executes it with military precision. But product development isn’t about executing a fixed plan; it’s about discovery, iteration, and problem-solving in environments where requirements constantly evolve.

唉，并不。James 和 Juan 都在餐饮业干过。说真的，Juan 在“堕入黑暗面”之前就是个职业厨师，而厨师团队制恰恰是一个“如何不去协作交付产品”的反面教材。团队制那种森严的等级和僵化的角色划分，在做产品时常常失灵。团队制是为执行和重复而设计的，不是为创造。餐厅后厨的首要目标是夜夜都按规格反复做出同样的菜。主厨设计菜单，其他人以军事般的精确去执行。但产品开发不是执行一份固定计划，而是在需求不断演变的环境里去发现、迭代、解决问题。

The brigade system’s strict hierarchy stifles the very things that product teams need most: cross-functional collaboration, creative problem-solving, and rapid adaptation.

团队制那种森严的等级，恰恰扼杀了产品团队最需要的东西：跨职能协作、创造性的问题解决，以及快速适应。

— 原书第 197 页 —

In a traditional kitchen, a line cook who suggests improvements to a dish might be told, “Just cook it as directed.” But that mindset is deadly in product development, where the best solutions often come from unexpected places and from the team members who are closest to specific problems.

在传统后厨里，一个想改进某道菜的打荷可能会被告知：“照指示做就行。”但这种心态在产品开发中是致命的——最好的方案往往来自意料之外的地方，来自离具体问题最近的团队成员。

The knowledge silos created by strict station assignments are another major issue. In a brigade, the saucier might not know much about pastry, and that’s considered acceptable. But in product development, when a backend engineer is the only one who understands the data model, or a frontend engineer is the only one who knows the UI framework, you’ve created dangerous dependencies and bottlenecks. When that person gets sick, goes on vacation, or leaves, the entire product suffers.

由严格岗位划分造成的知识孤岛是另一个大问题。在团队制里，酱汁师可能对甜点一窍不通，这被认为是可接受的。但在产品开发中，当某个后端工程师是唯一懂数据模型的人，或某个前端工程师是唯一懂 UI 框架的人，你就制造了危险的依赖和瓶颈。一旦那个人生病、度假或离职，整个产品都要遭殃。

In Practice: April’s Story

实践案例：April 的故事

April discovered the studio operations team’s communication breakdown through a critical incident. The authentication service (Marcus’s domain) failed at 2:00 a.m. This resulted in Derek and Sarah spending four hours debugging because Marcus hadn’t documented the custom JWT rotation scheme that he implemented. When Marcus returned from vacation, he fixed it in five minutes. The post-assessment revealed similar patterns everywhere: Sarah’s React components used an undocumented state management pattern that only she understood, Derek’s database had stored procedures with cryptic names like “sp_process_thing_v2_final_FINAL.” So, April implemented “Documentation Fridays,” where the last two hours of every Friday are dedicated to documenting one piece of institutional knowledge. She made it stick by having each senior engineer present their documentation to the juniors, who asked questions until they could operate the systems themselves.

April 是通过一次重大故障才发现工作室运营团队的沟通崩盘的。凌晨 2 点，认证服务（Marcus 的地盘）挂了。Derek 和 Sarah 花了四个小时调试，就因为 Marcus 没把他自己实现的那套自定义 JWT 轮换方案写下来。Marcus 度假回来后，五分钟就修好了。事后复盘发现到处都是同款问题：Sarah 的 React 组件用了一种没写文档、只有她自己懂的状态管理模式；Derek 的数据库里一堆名字莫名其妙的存储过程，比如“sp_process_thing_v2_final_FINAL”。于是 April 搞了“文档星期五&rdquo&rdquo：每周五最后两个小时专门用来把一条组织知识写下来。她让这事真正落地的办法是，让每位资深工程师向初级工程师讲解自己写的文档，初级工程师不断提问，直到自己能独立操作为止。

The command-and-control communication style is the most problematic aspect. “Yes, chef!” might keep a dinner service moving, but it doesn’t encourage the questioning and challenging that are necessary for innovation. James has seen countless product teams fail because they adopted this top-down approach, where decisions flowed from leadership without meaningful input from those doing the implementation work.

命令与控制式的沟通风格是最成问题的一环。“是，主厨！”也许能让晚餐服务转起来，但它并不鼓励创新所必需的质疑与挑战。James 见过无数产品团队失败，原因就是采用了这种自上而下的方式——决策从领导层流出，那些真正动手实现的人却没有有意义的 input。

Modern product development thrives on cross-functional teams where boundaries blur, roles overlap, and everyone contributes to both problem definition and solution. Engineers need to understand user needs, designers need to grasp technical constraints, and product managers need to appreciate both. The brigade’s neat separation of duties simply doesn’t work when building complex products in uncertain environments.

现代产品开发依赖于跨职能团队而蓬勃发展：边界模糊、角色交叠，每个人既参与定义问题，也参与解决问题。工程师需要理解用户需求，设计师需要把握技术约束，产品经理则需要两者都体会。在不确定的环境中构建复杂产品时，团队制那种干净利落的职责划分根本行不通。

— 原书第 198 页 —

We discussed some of these ways of working in Chapter 6.
其中一些工作方式我们在第 6 章讨论过。

So, while there’s certainly value in clear responsibilities and coordination, successful product teams look less like military brigades and more like jazz ensembles; individual expertise combined with collaborative improvisation, guided by shared objectives rather than rigid hierarchies. They maintain enough structure to stay coordinated but remain fluid enough to respond to the changing needs of users and markets.

所以，尽管清晰的职责划分与协调确有其价值，成功的产品团队看上去更像爵士乐团，而不是军事旅队：个人专长加上协作式即兴演奏，由共同目标而非僵化等级来引导。它们保持足够的结构以维持协调，又足够灵活以回应用户和市场不断变化的需求。

Saying that this is easy is one thing, but getting there is much harder. So let’s talk about how you can achieve this.

说“这很容易”是一回事，真正做到难得多。那我们就来谈谈你该如何做到。

Communicate, Communicate, Communicate

沟通、沟通、再沟通

Communication forms the backbone of effective technical collaboration. In chaotic environments, where requirements shift and priorities change daily, getting communication right is what separates teams that excel from teams that struggle. As we discussed in Chapter 3, teams must develop deliberate communication strategies. These strategies need to account for the complex nature of technical work, the informational density of many of the concepts, and ensure that a diverse community of cross-functional collaborators all get on the same page.

沟通是有效技术协作的脊梁。在需求每日漂移、优先级天天变化的混乱环境里，把沟通做对，正是卓越团队与挣扎团队的分水岭。正如第 3 章所讨论的，团队必须制定有意识的沟通策略。这些策略需要顾及技术工作的复杂性、许多概念的信息密度，并确保一个多元的、跨职能的协作者社群都能对齐到同一页上。

Building software can be incredibly complex, which means we have a wide range of potential communication pitfalls and barriers that can appear—sometimes from multiple sources—at the same time. Technical jargon creates walls between specialists and generalists. Distributed teams struggle with time zone differences and the loss of nonverbal cues. High-pressure, chaotic environments can lead to terse, easily misinterpreted messages. Addressing these barriers requires deliberate effort to create communication norms that work for the team.

构建软件可能极其复杂，这意味着我们面对的沟通陷阱和障碍五花八门，而且常常同时——甚至来自多个源头——出现。技术黑话在专才与通才之间筑起高墙。分布式团队受困于时区差异和非语言线索的丢失。高压、混乱的环境会导致消息简短、极易被误读。要破除这些障碍，需要有意识地努力，建立适合本团队的沟通规范。

As we’ve discovered, communication isn’t just about transferring information; it’s about creating a shared context. As your team and products grow, the risk of context loss increases dramatically. New team members join without the historical understanding that guided initial decisions. Engineers can become siloed and focus intensely on their domains without seeing broader connections. This fragmentation of knowledge leads to misaligned efforts and inefficient solutions. Great technical leaders—both engineering leaders and individual contributors—recognize that their job isn’t just to share information but to create a coherent narrative that connects individual contributions to the larger mission.

正如我们发现的，沟通不只是传递信息，更是创造共享上下文。随着团队和产品壮大，上下文丢失的风险急剧上升。新成员加入时，并不了解那些当初指导决策的历史背景。工程师可能被孤岛化，死死盯着自己的领域，看不到更宏观的关联。这种知识的碎裂会导致努力方向不一致、方案低效。优秀的技术领导者——无论是工程管理者还是个人贡献者——都明白：他们的工作不只是分享信息，而是编织一条连贯的叙事，把个人贡献连接到更大的使命上。

— 原书第 199 页 —

Cadences

沟通节奏

So, we start by establishing clear communication cadences that help maintain alignment without drowning teams in meetings. Daily check-ins provide quick course corrections, weekly syncs enable deeper problem-solving, and monthly reviews connect technical work to broader business objectives. These structured touchpoints create predictable information flows, reducing uncertainty and helping teams stay coordinated without constant interruptions.

于是，我们先从建立清晰的沟通节奏入手：既维持对齐，又不让团队淹在会议里。每日站会做快速纠偏，每周同步做更深入的问题解决，每月复盘把技术工作和更宏观的业务目标连起来。这些结构化的触点创造了可预期的信息流，减少不确定性，让团队不必被不停打断也能保持协调。

It’s hard to provide a calendar or agenda for good cadences, as they vary from team to team and are mediated by time zones and geographies. What we can tell you is that if you poll your team and ask “Do you know what you need to know?” and the answer is “No” or just a look of panic, then looking at how frequently you share information is a good starting point to solve the issue.

要给出一套放之四海皆准的日程或议程很难，因为节奏因团队而异，还受时区和地理分布影响。我们能告诉你的是：如果你去问团队“你们知道自己需要知道的事吗？”，而答案是“不知道”、或者只是一脸惊慌，那么检视一下你分享信息的频率，就是解决问题的好起点。

Mediums and modalities

媒介与方式

We also need to be flexible about the medium or mediums of these communications. James has witnessed this firsthand, repeatedly, when leading distributed teams across multiple continents. Initially, teams tend to rely primarily on one form of communication: we meet weekly via video conference or write documentation. However, time zones, cultural differences, and individual preferences in communication styles quickly lead to frequent misunderstandings and gaps. The only way to fix this is by establishing a multimodal approach—for example, using synchronous video for complex discussions, asynchronous audio messages for nuanced explanations (everyone loves a podcast!), and written documents for reference. This will dramatically reduce communication failures. The key is recognizing the following:

我们还需要在沟通媒介上保持灵活。James 在带领横跨多个大洲的分布式团队时，反复亲历了这一点。起初，团队往往主要依赖某一种沟通形式：要么每周视频会议，要么写文档。然而时区差异、文化差异以及沟通风格上的个人偏好，很快就会导致频繁的误解和信息缺口。解决之道只有一个：建立多模态（multimodal）的方式——比如复杂讨论用同步视频，需要细腻解释的用异步语音消息（谁不喜欢播客呢！），供查阅的内容用书面文档。这会大幅减少沟通失败。关键是要认识到以下几点：

  • Different types of information flow more effectively through different channels.

    不同类型的信息，通过不同渠道流动得更顺畅。

  • Different types of information are consumed differently by different people and teams.

    不同类型的信息，被不同的人和团队以不同方式消化。

  • Different types of information are more sensitive to external pressures, like time zones, language, and cultural differences.

    不同类型的信息，对外部压力（如时区、语言和文化差异）的敏感度也不同。

So, we need to create norms that match the medium to the message. For technical teams, in particular, choosing the right communication tools can make all the difference. Architecture discussions benefit from visual collaboration tools with real-time diagramming capabilities. Design, architecture, or API contract negotiations work best with structured documentation tools that track changes and discussions. Day-to-day coordination might happen in persistent chat tools with organized threads and searchable history. The most successful teams don’t just pick tools haphazardly; they thoughtfully match communication channels to the types of information being exchanged. They also multicast the information via multiple mediums.

因此，我们需要建立让“媒介匹配信息”的规范。尤其对技术团队来说，选对沟通工具可能天差地别。架构讨论适合用带实时画图能力的可视化协作工具。设计、架构或 API 契约协商，最适合用能追踪变更和讨论的结构化文档工具。日常协调则可以在持久化聊天工具里进行——话题组织清晰、历史可搜。最成功的团队不是随意挑工具，而是深思熟虑地把沟通渠道与所交换信息的类型相匹配。他们还会通过多种媒介把信息多播（multicast）出去。

— 原书第 200 页 —

But you’re going to spam people! Well, no—spamming people is sending the same information multiple times via the same medium. “I sent the email six times,” is pretty much guaranteed to result in someone ignoring your email. But sending an email, a Slack update, updating a Notion document, and reiterating in a video conference are not spamming, but rather multicasting.
可你这是在骚扰大家！其实不是——骚扰，是用同一种媒介把同一条信息发好几遍。“我把邮件发了六遍”，几乎注定会有人直接无视你的邮件。但发一封邮件、更一条Slack、更新一个 Notion 文档、再在视频会上重申一遍，这不是骚扰，而是多播。

Visualizations

可视化

While the argument that most humans are visual learners is probably false, there’s no denying that visual information can dramatically speed up understanding of complex technical concepts. Visuals work because they bypass the limitations of serial processing in text and speech. Our brains process visual information holistically and in parallel, making it easier to grasp relationships, hierarchies, and patterns. That’s why an exemplary architecture diagram can convey more meaning than pages of explanation, and why whiteboarding remains the go-to activity when technical folk get stuck.

尽管“大多数人都是视觉型学习者”这个说法大概站不住脚，但不可否认，视觉信息能极大加快对复杂技术概念的理解。可视化之所以有效，是因为它绕开了文字和语音那种串行处理的局限。我们的大脑以整体、并行的方式处理视觉信息，从而更容易把握关系、层级和模式。这就是为什么一张出色的架构图能比好几页文字说明传达更多含义，也是为什么技术人卡住时，白板讨论永远是首选活动。

But not all visualizations are created equal. Compelling technical visuals strike a balance between simplicity and accuracy. James once worked with a group of architects whose diagrams were so detailed and comprehensive that they became as impenetrable as the systems they tried to explain. The best technical visualizations follow the principle of progressive disclosure—showing the big picture first, and then enabling viewers to drill down into details as needed.

但并非所有可视化都生而平等。有说服力的技术图在简洁与准确之间取得平衡。James 曾和一群架构师共事，他们的图详尽完备到了这种程度：和它们想要解释的系统一样让人看不懂。最好的技术可视化遵循“渐进披露”原则——先展示全貌，再让观看者按需下钻到细节。

Consider using tools like Miro, Figma, and LucidChart, or hybrid tools like Mermaid, that enable you to embed visuals in other tools. These, or indeed any drawing tool, have transformed how teams create and share visuals. The collaborative aspects of these platforms mean that diagrams become living artifacts that teams build together rather than static images created by a single person. When visuals become collaborative, they better represent a shared understanding than individual perspectives.

可以考虑用 Miro、Figma、LucidChart 这类工具，或 Mermaid 这种能把图嵌入其他工具的混合工具。它们——或者说任何画图工具——已经改变了团队创建和分享可视化的方式。这些平台的协作属性意味着：图变成了大家共同构建的“活的”产物，而不是某个人画完的静态图片。当可视化变成协作式的，它所代表的就更接近共同理解，而非个人视角。

Standardize your visual language across the team. Whether you’re using Unified Modeling Language (UML), C4, or your custom notation, consistency helps everyone interpret diagrams correctly. Also, be consistent in using colors. And don’t forget that ~8% of the population has color vision deficiency.
在全团队统一你的可视化语言。无论你用的是统一建模语言（UML）、C4，还是自定义记号，一致性都能帮每个人正确读图。颜色的使用也要一致。另外别忘了，约 8% 的人存在色觉缺陷。

Video calls

视频会议

The pandemic normalized video calls as a primary communication channel, but most teams still haven’t figured out how to make them truly effective. Video calls enable you to convey emotion, build relationships, and handle complex discussions where facial expressions and tone matter. They’re far from perfect, but they represent the best possible substitute for real-time, in-person interaction. They are, however,

疫情让视频会议成为一种常规的主要沟通渠道，但大多数团队仍没搞懂如何让它真正高效。视频会议让你能传递情绪、建立关系，并处理那些面部表情和语气很重要的复杂讨论。它远非完美，却是实时面对面交流的最佳替代。不过，它

— 原书第 201 页 —

broadly terrible for detailed technical work and deep problem-solving unless carefully structured. Slides deserve a special callout here. For most video calls, slides render all the benefits of interaction—however limited they are—completely worthless. Despite the temptation, avoid slides. Please.

在没有精心设计结构的情况下，用于细致的技术工作和深度问题解决时，总体上很糟糕。幻灯片这里要特别点名批评。对大多数视频会议而言，幻灯片会把互动带来的那点好处（哪怕本来就有限）彻底清零。尽管很想这么做，还是别用幻灯片。拜托了。

High-performing technical teams approach video differently. They use video strategically, rather than as a default, and they structure calls to take advantage of the medium’s strengths. For quick status updates or information sharing, asynchronous tools are usually better; save video for conversations that benefit from real-time interaction and emotional connection.

高绩效的技术团队对视频的用法不同。他们有策略地使用视频，而不是默认一切都开会；他们给会议做结构设计，以发挥这种媒介的长处。快速的状态同步或信息分享，用异步工具通常更好；把视频留给那些能从实时互动和情感连接中获益的对话。

In the past, we’ve seen people use video to build relationships across globally distributed engineering organizations. For example, when James was at Kickstarter, an app called “Coffee Roulette” was developed that matched people across the organization who didn’t work together or might not have met. The company paid for them to have a (physical) coffee together. This concept can be extended to be global and remote: “virtual coffee” sessions with optional 30-minute video calls. The company buys you a pastry and coffee or the like, and off you go—no agenda beyond getting to know each other.

过去我们见过有人用视频在全球分布式的工程组织里建立关系。例如 James 在 Kickstarter 时，公司开发了一个叫“咖啡轮盘”的应用，把组织里互不共事、可能素未谋面的人配对。公司出钱让他们一起喝杯（现实中的）咖啡。这个概念可以扩展到全球远程场景：“虚拟咖啡”时段，可选 30 分钟视频通话。公司给你买块点心和一杯咖啡之类的，然后你们就开聊——除了互相认识之外没有任何议程。

For technical discussions, the most effective video calls incorporate shared visual spaces. Tools like meeting apps with whiteboard features, screen sharing with drawing capabilities, or integration with collaborative design tools can transform passive listening into active collaboration.

对技术讨论而言，最有效的视频会议会引入共享的视觉空间。带白板功能的会议应用、带标注能力的屏幕共享、或与协作设计工具的集成，都能把被动听讲变成主动协作。

Most importantly, great teams establish explicit video call norms. Camera expectations, muting practices, and participation signals can reduce the cognitive overhead of video interaction. For example, raising hands for attention or to show reactions helps keep conversations flowing and limits the potential for derailment.

最重要的是，优秀团队会建立明确的视频会议规范。对摄像头的要求、静音习惯、参与信号，都能降低视频互动的认知负担。比如举手示意或用举手表达反应，有助于让对话顺畅进行，并减少跑题的可能。

Audio

音频

Audio remains the unsung hero of technical communication. While video dominates synchronous remote interaction and text dominates asynchronous exchanges, audio offers some cool benefits that we suggest you explore.

音频始终是技术沟通里那位无名英雄。当视频主导着同步远程互动、文字主导着异步交流时，音频提供了一些很酷的好处，我们建议你去发掘。

Voice messages deliver nuance and emotion more effectively than text without requiring the scheduling and full attention that video calls demand. An interesting potential use is asynchronous voice messages for code reviews that involve significant feedback. When an engineer needs to explain why a particular approach might cause issues, a two-minute voice note conveys both technical concerns and a supportive tone in a way that text comments often fail to do.

语音消息比文字更有效地传递细微差别和情绪，又不像视频会议那样需要预约时间和全神贯注。一个有趣的潜在用途是：对那些包含大量反馈的代码评审，用异步语音消息来沟通。当一位工程师需要解释为什么某个做法可能出问题时，一段两分钟的语音便能同时传达技术上的担忧和支持的语气——这是文字评论往往做不到的。

Recorded technical discussions create valuable learning resources with minimal additional effort. Simply recording architecture discussions or technical planning sessions creates an archive that new team members can consume at their own pace. With

录制下来的技术讨论，只需极少额外付出，就能创造宝贵的学习资源。只要把架构讨论或技术规划会议录下来，就形成了一个档案库，新人可以按自己的节奏去消化。借助

— 原书第 202 页 —

AI and transcription you can also turn these recordings into documents or even summarized into an architectural design record (ADR). Some teams even record pair-programming sessions on key components or addressing common challenges in a codebase—an invaluable resource for onboarding that requires virtually no extra work.

AI 和转录工具，你还能把这些录像转成文档，甚至总结成一份架构设计记录（ADR）。有些团队甚至录制关键组件上的结对编程、或讲解代码库中常见挑战的环节——这对新人入职来说是无价的资源，而几乎不需要额外工作。

Podcasts and audio lunch-and-learns offer accessible, continuous learning opportunities. One engineer whom James worked with started recording short technical explainers about their system architecture while driving to work. Combined with a few simple hand-drawn sketches, these ended up as supplements to the documentation.

播客和音频版的“午餐学习会”提供了触手可及、持续不断的学习机会。James 共事过的一位工程师，开始在开车上班时录制关于本系统架构的短小讲解。配上几幅简单的手绘草图，这些录音最后成了文档的补充材料。

Audio’s biggest strength might be its compatibility with other activities. Unlike reading or watching a video, which demands visual attention, audio can be consumed while doing other things like taking a walk or making lunch. This makes it particularly valuable for teams feeling overwhelmed by information; audio offers a way to keep learning and stay connected without adding more screen time to already overloaded days. When James feels overwhelmed with activities, he often breaks, leaves his office, and listens to a recorded meeting that he couldn’t attend (though normal people would or should just listen to a podcast).

音频最大的长处或许是它能和其他活动兼容。阅读或看视频需要占用视觉注意力，音频却可以在你散步、做午饭之类的事情时顺便听。这对被信息压得喘不过气的团队尤其有价值：音频提供了一种方式，让你在已经过载的一天里不必再增加屏幕时间，也能持续学习、保持连接。当 James 觉得日程被压得喘不过气时，他常常起身离开办公室，去听一场自己没能参加的会议的录音（当然，正常人大概会、也应该去听播客）。

Chat and messaging

聊天与即时消息

Chat tools like Slack, Discord, and (sigh) even Microsoft Teams have transformed day-to-day technical communication, creating persistent and searchable conversation spaces that blend synchronous and asynchronous interactions. When used thoughtfully, these platforms dramatically reduce email overload and create more inclusive conversations. When used poorly, they become overwhelming firehoses of disorganized information.

Slack、Discord 乃至（叹气）Microsoft Teams 这类聊天工具，已经改变了日常技术沟通：它们创造了持久、可搜索的对话空间，把同步和异步互动融合在一起。用得好时，这些平台能大幅减轻邮件过载，营造更包容的对话氛围。用得糟时，它们就成了吞没你的、毫无条理的信息消防水龙。

Effective teams create intentional structure in their chat environments. Rather than having general channels that become noise factories, they create purpose-built spaces with explicit scopes. And they create those spaces iteratively. If you don’t need a channel yet, then don’t create one until it becomes clear that the conversation needs its own home. Juan is a particular exponent of carefully named channels using prefixes:

高效的团队会在聊天环境中刻意设计结构。他们不会搞一堆变成噪音工厂的通用频道，而是建立有明确范围的、用途专门的空间。而且这些空间是迭代着建起来的。如果你还不需要某个频道，就先别建，直到某场对话明显需要一个自己的家为止。Juan 尤其推崇用前缀来精心命名频道：

  • Team- For channels for specific teams

    Team- 用于特定团队的频道

  • Proj- For particular projects

    Proj- 用于特定项目

  • Ext- For channels with external parties

    Ext- 用于与外部方沟通的频道

— 原书第 203 页 —

Well-structured threads keep conversations coherent without splintering team awareness. Teams with strong threading habits maintained much more transparent communication even as they scaled. The simple practice of responding in threads rather than the main channel prevented conversations from overlapping while preserving context.

结构良好的话题串能让对话保持连贯，又不至于割裂团队的整体认知。有良好串聊习惯的团队，即便规模扩大，沟通也保持得透明得多。“在话题串里回复、而不是在主频道里回复”这个简单做法，既避免了多场对话互相重叠，又保留了上下文。

Chat also creates valuable opportunities for personality and team culture to shine through. Emoji reactions, GIFs, and informal banter might seem trivial, but they build essential social bonds in distributed teams. Both James and Juan like to establish channels like a pets channel, a chatter channel where people can say hi and talk about their day, and a channel for new folk to introduce themselves. There is even a “weird-Australian-s***” channel in one of Juan and James’ Slack channels, where the small community of Australians in the team share the weird and wonderful aspects of Australia that seem to bewilder and charm Americans (and yes, the spiders are that big).

聊天还为个性和团队文化提供了宝贵的展示舞台。表情回应、GIF 和闲聊看似琐碎，但在分布式团队里它们构筑了至关重要的社会纽带。James 和 Juan 都喜欢建一些频道：晒宠物的频道、打招呼聊日常的闲聊频道、让新人做自我介绍的频道。在 Juan 和 James 共用的某个 Slack 里，甚至还有一个“奇怪澳大利亚玩意儿”频道，团队里那一小群澳大利亚人在上面分享澳洲那些让美国人既困惑又着迷的奇趣之处（没错，蜘蛛真有那么大）。

Most importantly, high-functioning teams establish healthy expectations around chat response times and availability. The always-on nature of messaging platforms can create unhealthy pressure without explicit norms.

最重要的是，高运转的团队会就聊天的响应时间和在线状态建立健康的预期。即时通讯平台那种“永远在线”的特性，如果没有明确规范，会造成不健康的压力。

Email

电子邮件

Email might feel like (is?) the dinosaur of technical communication tools, but it remains surprisingly resilient for good reasons. Unlike the constant stream of chat or the ephemeral nature of conversations, email creates a persistent, searchable record with built-in threading that works across organizational boundaries. Despite predictions of its demise, email continues to serve vital functions in the communication ecosystems of technical teams.

电子邮件感觉上（或者说事实上？）像是技术沟通工具里的恐龙，但它出人意料地顽强存活，而且理由充分。和聊天那种永不停歇的信息流、或对话那种转瞬即逝的性质不同，邮件创造了一份持久、可搜索、自带话题串的记录，而且能跨组织边界使用。尽管一再有人预言它将消亡，邮件仍在技术团队的沟通生态中承担着关键职能。

Where email truly shines is in communications that need formality, a paper trail, or external reach. Email remains the universal connector across organizational boundaries, making it invaluable for technical discussions that extend beyond your immediate team.

邮件真正发光的地方，是那些需要正式性、需要书面留痕、或需要触达外部的沟通。它依然是跨越组织边界的通用连接器，对于超出你直属团队范围的技术讨论来说，价值不可替代。

Email’s asynchronous nature and reduced urgency expectations make it well suited for thoughtful, nonurgent communication. We’ve found that technical discussions in email tend to be more carefully considered than the rapid-fire exchanges in chat tools. For complex technical proposals or detailed feedback that requires careful wording, email provides space for reflection that faster-paced channels don’t encourage. Email also has numerous automation shortcuts: categories, tags/labels, and folders, and most modern email suites have the ability to decorate and route emails using their source, destination, subject, etc.

邮件的异步特性和较低的紧迫感预期，使它非常适合深思熟虑、不紧急的沟通。我们发现，邮件里的技术讨论往往比聊天工具里那种噼里啪啦的往返更经过斟酌。对于复杂的技术提案、或需要仔细措辞的详细反馈，邮件提供了快节奏渠道所不鼓励的反思空间。邮件还有大量自动化捷径：分类、标签、文件夹；大多数现代邮件套件都能根据发件人、收件人、主题等来给邮件加装饰、做路由。

However, email’s weaknesses are well-known and significant. Its one-to-many broadcasting nature can create overwhelming inbox volume when misused. Teams that default to “Reply all” for routine acknowledgments often find themselves

然而，邮件的弱点同样广为人知且相当严重。它那种一对多的广播特性一旦被滥用，会造成收件箱邮件爆炸。那些对日常确认也习惯性“回复所有人”的团队，常常发现自己

— 原书第 204 页 —

overwhelmed with low-value messages. The same applies to notifications from code reviews or observability systems—too many of them, and alert fatigue sets in, causing emails to be ignored.

被一堆低价值消息淹没。代码评审或可观测系统的通知也是同理——太多了，就会出现告警疲劳，导致邮件被无视。

Another common pitfall is using email for real-time coordination or discussions that require rapid iteration. Email’s inherent latency makes it poorly suited for dynamic conversations. If your email thread is 10+ emails long, then maybe a different medium is needed. Recognizing when to move conversations to more appropriate channels is a crucial skill for effective communication.

另一个常见陷阱是：把邮件用于实时协调、或需要快速迭代的讨论。邮件固有的延迟使它很不适合动态对话。如果你的邮件串已经超过 10 封，也许就该换个媒介了。能识别出什么时候该把对话搬到更合适的渠道，是有效沟通的一项关键技能。

The most successful teams view email as a specialized tool rather than a default. They establish clear guidelines about what belongs in email versus chat, documentation systems, or synchronous conversations. Despite newer tools with flashier features, email’s staying power comes from its universality, flexibility, and familiarity. Rather than trying to eliminate it, aim to thoughtfully integrate email into the ecosystem, leveraging its strengths while compensating for its weaknesses with other channels.

最成功的团队把邮件当作一种专用工具，而不是默认选项。他们就“什么该走邮件、什么该走聊天、文档系统或同步对话”建立清晰的指引。尽管新工具功能更炫酷，邮件之所以经久不衰，靠的是它的普遍性、灵活性和熟悉度。与其试图消灭它，不如有意识地把它整合进生态：发挥它的长处，同时用其他渠道弥补它的短处。

In-person interactions

面对面交流

Despite the rise of remote work, in-person interaction remains uniquely powerful for certain types of technical communication. The richness of face-to-face discussion—with its natural turn-taking, subtle nonverbal cues, and shared physical context—makes it especially valuable for complex problem-solving and building relationships. In our humble opinion, whiteboarding sessions continue to outperform digital equivalents for fluid ideation and system design. The combination of an ample visual space, physical movement, and immediate feedback loops creates a creative environment that is difficult to replicate virtually. Even teams that are mostly remote will find tremendous value in occasional in-person architecture or design sessions.

尽管远程办公兴起，面对面交流对某些类型的技术沟通而言仍具有独特的威力。面对面讨论的丰富性——自然的轮流发言、微妙的非语言线索、共享的物理场景——使它对复杂问题解决和建立关系格外有价值。在我们看来，就流畅的构思和系统设计而言，白板讨论至今仍胜过数字等价物。充足的视觉空间、身体的移动、即时的反馈回路，三者结合营造出一种在线上难以复制的创造氛围。即便主要是远程的团队，也会发现偶尔的线下架构或设计会议价值巨大。

Pair programming takes on new dimensions when two engineers share physical space. The reduced friction in switching who’s typing, the ease of pointing at specific parts of the screen, and the natural conversation flow make in-person pairing particularly effective for knowledge transfer and tackling thorny bugs.

当两位工程师共处一室时，结对编程会展现出新的维度。切换谁来敲键盘的摩擦更小、指着屏幕某一处更方便、对话也更自然流畅——这些让线下结对在知识传递和攻克棘手 bug 时格外有效。

Informal interactions around the office create invaluable serendipitous knowledge sharing. The classic “overheard conversation at the coffee machine” that solves a problem someone didn’t even know they had might seem like a cliché. Still, these moments genuinely build team cohesion and cross-pollinate ideas.

办公室里的非正式互动会创造无价的、不期而遇的知识分享。那种“在咖啡机旁偶然听到的对话，顺手解决了一个当事人自己都没意识到的问题”，听起来像陈词滥调。但这些时刻确实能凝聚团队、让想法交叉授粉。

For distributed teams that can’t meet in person regularly, off-site gatherings become even more crucial. Targeted team gatherings every few months provide the foundation for relationship building that makes all other communication channels more effective. The most successful off-sites will balance structured technical work with unstructured social time, recognizing that both contribute to better collaboration.

对于无法定期线下相聚的分布式团队，异地团建（off-site）就变得愈发关键。每隔几个月一次、有目标的团队聚会，为建立关系打下基础，进而让其他所有沟通渠道都更高效。最成功的 off-site 会在结构化技术工作与非结构化社交时间之间取得平衡，因为两者都有助于更好的协作。

— 原书第 205 页 —

Documentation

文档

Documentation plays a critical role in technical communication, serving as an external memory for the team. But documentation is only valuable if it’s read and used. Let’s face it—great code with terrible documentation isn’t great code; it’s a future nightmare waiting to happen. The moment your star engineer wins the lottery and moves to Bali, that undocumented authentication service becomes a ticking time bomb.

文档在技术沟通中扮演关键角色，是团队的外部记忆。但文档只有在被人读、被人用时才有价值。咱们说实话：代码很棒、文档很烂，那不叫很棒的代码，那是一颗等着引爆的未来噩梦。当你的明星工程师中了彩票搬去巴厘岛那一刻，那个没写文档的认证服务就成了一颗定时炸弹。

Successful teams view documentation not as a tedious checkbox exercise, but as a form of time travel—with messages sent to future team members, including their future selves. James once worked with a team that had a security incident, and then had to reverse-engineer their API to fix it because the original engineers had moved on without documenting it. What should have been a quick intervention took three weeks of archaeological code excavation and iterative change as new things were learned and discoveries made. After this painful experience, they adopted a “documentation as you go” approach (and wrote tests) because no one wanted to go through that experience again.

成功的团队不把文档看成烦人的打勾任务，而是一种时间旅行——给未来的团队成员（包括未来的自己）捎去的信。James 曾共事过一支团队，出过一次安全事故，结果不得不反向工程自己的 API 才能修好它——因为最初写它的工程师早已离职，什么文档都没留。本应快速处置的问题，花了三周的“考古式”代码挖掘和反复修改，边学边发现新情况。这次惨痛经历之后，他们采用了“边做边写文档”的做法（还写了测试），因为没人想再经历一遍。

Different types of documentation serve different purposes, and recognizing these distinctions helps teams create more valuable resources. Reference documentation—such as API specs, function signatures, and database schemas—benefits from automation and standardization. Conceptual documentation (e.g., architecture overviews, design rationales, and mental models) requires thoughtful human explanation accompanied by plenty of visuals. Procedural documentation (setup instructions, troubleshooting guides, operational runbooks) needs clear, step-by-step sequences with examples. Teams that try to treat all documentation the same way often end up with resources that serve no purpose.

不同类型的文档服务于不同目的，认清这些区别能帮团队创造更有价值的资料。参考类文档（如 API 规格、函数签名、数据库 schema）适合自动化和标准化。概念类文档（如架构概览、设计 rationale、心智模型）需要人来深思熟虑地讲解，并配以大量图示。流程类文档（安装说明、排障指南、运维手册）则需要清晰的、带示例的一步步操作序列。试图用同一套方式对待所有文档的团队，最后往往做出一堆毫无用处的资料。

The perennial challenge is keeping documentation fresh as systems evolve. Static documentation inevitably drifts from reality, sometimes becoming worse than no documentation at all by leading engineers down incorrect paths. We’re big fans of collocating documentation and code. Moving critical documentation directly into the codebase and into places like pull request templates puts it front and center. We also recommend including documentation updates into the definition of “done”; if the docs are not updated, then the team can’t claim that they have completed the fix or feature. The best documentation lives where the work happens, whether that’s in code comments, README files, or tools that engineers use daily.

长久的挑战是：随着系统演进，如何让文档保持新鲜。静态文档不可避免地会与现实脱节，有时比没有文档还糟——因为它会把工程师带上错误的路。我们非常推崇把文档和代码放在一起。把关键文档直接搬进代码库、放进 Pull Request 模板之类的地方，让它走到台前。我们还建议把“更新文档”纳入“完成”的定义；如果文档没更新，团队就不能宣称这个修复或功能已经做完。最好的文档就活在工作发生的地方——无论是代码注释、README，还是工程师每天都用的工具里。

Effective documentation strikes a balance between comprehensiveness and conciseness. The sweet spot is documentation that answers the most essential questions clearly and points to where more details can be found if needed. There is an adage (that neither of us can remember the origin of): “Document the ‘why’ thoroughly, the ‘what’ clearly, and the ‘how’ only when it’s not obvious from the code.”

有效的文档在全面与简洁之间取得平衡。最佳点在于：文档能清晰回答最核心的问题，并在需要时指出哪里能找到更多细节。有一句格言（我俩都记不清出处了）：“把‘为什么’写透，把‘是什么’写清，‘怎么做’只在代码里看不出来时才写。”

— 原书第 206 页 —

The best teams establish clear ownership of documentation without making it the sole responsibility of one person. Making documentation enjoyable to create and consume pays enormous dividends. Teams that view documentation as a creative challenge rather than a burden tend to produce resources that get used.

最好的团队会为文档确立清晰的责任人，又不把它变成某一个人的专属负担。让写文档、读文档都变成一件愉快的事，会带来巨大回报。那些把文档看作创造性挑战而非负担的团队，往往能产出真正被人使用的资料。

Finally, a documentation culture requires leadership investment and setting an example. When senior engineers and architects treat documentation as optional or low priority, then junior team members will follow suit. When leaders explicitly value clear explanation alongside working code—by celebrating good documentation, allocating time for creating it, and visibly using it themselves—they establish norms that strengthen the team’s collective knowledge base.

最后，文档文化需要领导层投入并以身作则。当资深工程师和架构师把文档当成可有可无、低优先级的事，初级成员就会有样学样。当领导者明确地把“清晰的解释”与“能跑的代码”同等看待——表彰好文档、为写文档分配时间、自己也 visibly 地使用文档——他们就建立起了强化团队集体知识库的规范。

Confirming understanding and handling disagreement

确认理解与处理分歧

Communication isn’t complete until the message is received and understood, not just sent. In technical teams, this gap between transmission and reception causes countless problems: features built to the wrong specification, architectural decisions that surprise stakeholders, and teams working at cross-purposes despite regular meetings.

沟通只有在消息被接收并理解、而不只是被发送出去之后，才算完成。在技术团队里，发送与接收之间的这条鸿沟会造成无数问题：按错误规格造出的功能、让干系人意外的架构决策、以及尽管会议不断却仍各行其是的团队。

The first challenge is verification. How do you know that your message landed? Active confirmation techniques can help bridge this gap. After explaining a complex technical concept, ask team members to summarize it back in their own words. This isn’t meant to be patronizing; frame it as ensuring that you explained it well: “Let me check I’ve explained this clearly; how would you describe what we’re building to someone else?” For written communications, request explicit acknowledgment of key decisions or action items. A simple “Please confirm you’re aligned with this approach” prevents the silent disagreement that surfaces weeks later as rework.

第一个挑战是验证。你怎么知道自己的消息真的送到了？主动确认的技巧能帮你弥合这条鸿沟。在讲完一个复杂技术概念后，请团队成员用他们自己的话复述一遍。这不是要居高临下地对待人；把它框定为“确保我讲清楚了”：“我来确认一下我有没有讲明白——你会怎么跟别人描述我们正在做的东西？”对书面沟通，请对方对关键决策或待办事项给出明确确认。一句简单的“请确认你认同这个做法”，就能避免那种几周后才以返工形式冒出来的“沉默的反对”。

When people genuinely don’t understand despite multiple attempts, the problem usually isn’t their comprehension; it’s your explanation. Try switching modalities. If verbal explanation isn’t working, try visual diagrams. If documentation isn’t clicking, record a video walkthrough. Different people process information differently, and flexibility in your communication approach shows respect for these differences.

如果试了好几次别人还是真的不理解，问题通常不在他们的理解力，而在你的讲解。试着换一种方式。口头讲不通，就试试画图。文档看不进去，就录一段视频演示。不同的人处理信息的方式不同，沟通方式上的灵活本身就是对这些差异的尊重。

Disagreement requires even more nuance. There’s passive disagreement, where someone nods along but never truly buys in, and active disagreement, where concerns are voiced openly. Passive disagreement is more dangerous; it manifests as slow execution, subtle sabotage, or surprise objections late in the process. Create explicit opportunities for dissent: “What concerns do you have about this approach?” or “If you had to argue against this, what would you say?” Making disagreement safe and expected brings it into the open where it can be addressed.

处理分歧则需要更细腻的拿捏。有一种是被动的分歧——嘴上点头、心里从不真正认同；另一种是主动的分歧——担忧被公开说出来。被动分歧更危险；它表现为执行拖沓、暗中作梗，或在流程后期才突然跳出来反对。要主动创造表达异议的机会：“对这个做法你有什么顾虑？”或者“如果你要反对这件事，你会怎么说？”让分歧变得安全、变得可预期，才能把它摆到台面上加以处理。

When facing active disagreement, resist the urge to immediately counterargue. First, ensure you understand the objection completely. Repeat it back: “So your concern is that this approach won’t scale beyond 10,000 users; is that right?” Often, the act of clarification reveals that you’re not as far apart as initially thought. If genuine

面对主动分歧时，忍住立刻反驳的冲动。先确保你完全理解了对方的反对意见。把它复述回去：“所以你的顾虑是这个做法在超过一万用户时就扩展不了，是这样吗？”往往，澄清这一举动本身就会揭示：你们之间的分歧并没有一开始以为的那么大。如果确实

— 原书第 207 页 —

disagreement remains, acknowledge it explicitly and document it. “Sarah has raised concerns about scalability. We’re proceeding with this approach because we need to ship quickly, but we’ll revisit if user growth exceeds projections.” This shows you heard the concern and creates a clear trigger for reassessment.

仍存在真正的分歧，就明确承认并记录下来。“Sarah 对可扩展性提出了顾虑。我们之所以继续这个做法，是因为需要快速交付；但如果用户增长超出预期，我们会重新评估。”这既表明你听到了顾虑，也为将来的重新评估设下了一个明确的触发条件。

Sometimes, despite your best efforts, the message simply won’t land. After three failed attempts using different approaches, it’s time to escalate or find a translator—someone who can bridge the communication gap. This isn’t failure; it’s pragmatic recognition that sometimes a fresh voice or different relationship dynamic is what’s needed to break through.

有时你拼尽全力，消息就是送不到。换了三种方式都失败之后，就该升级处理、或找一个“翻译”——一个能弥合沟通鸿沟的人。这不是失败；这是务实地认识到：有时候，要打破僵局，需要的正是一个新的声音或一种不同的关系动态。

Transparency and ambiguity

透明与模糊

One of the primary challenges in technical communication is the inherent ambiguity that often characterizes chaotic settings. Teams must adapt to unclear situations while making purposeful decisions. This requires a careful balance of empowering team members to express their priorities and ensuring that decisions align with the overall project goals. Leadership plays a crucial role in shaping team dynamics and facilitating a culture that encourages collaborative decision making without imposing top-down directives.

技术沟通的主要挑战之一，是混乱环境中那种与生俱来的模糊性。团队必须适应不清晰的局面，同时做出有方向感的决策。这需要一种精妙的平衡：既赋能团队成员表达自己的优先级，又确保决策与项目整体目标对齐。在塑造团队动态、培育一种鼓励协作决策而非自上而下发号施令的文化方面，领导起着关键作用。

Ambiguity creates anxiety, and anxious teams tend to make poor decisions. Leaders can reduce this anxiety, not by pretending to have certainty where none exists, but by creating frameworks that help teams navigate uncertainty productively. This might include establishing transparent decision-making processes, defining what “good enough” looks like for different types of decisions, and creating spaces for structured speculation about possible futures.

模糊会制造焦虑，而焦虑的团队往往做出糟糕的决策。领导者要减轻这种焦虑，不是靠在根本没有确定性的地方假装确定，而是靠建立框架，帮团队建设性地穿越不确定性。这可能包括：建立透明的决策流程、为不同类型的决策定义“足够好”长什么样、以及创造空间让大家对各种可能的未来做结构化的推测。

Juan is fond of saying, “Default to open and public.” He can often be found lurking in Slack group chats, asking why this isn’t in a public channel. Creating a culture of transparent communication means recognizing that information is power, and that power should be distributed throughout the organization. When technical decisions happen behind closed doors or without proper context, teams feel disempowered and disconnected from the outcomes. By contrast, organizations that share information broadly—including the reasoning behind decisions, not just the decisions themselves—build trust and enable better autonomous decision making at all levels.

Juan 爱说一句话：“默认开放、公开。”你常常能看到他潜伏在 Slack 群聊里，追问这事为什么不在公开频道里。营造透明沟通的文化，意味着认识到信息就是权力，而这种权力应当在整个组织中分发。当技术决策在关门后做出、或缺乏恰当上下文时，团队会感到被剥夺了权力、与结果脱节。相反，广泛分享信息的组织——不仅分享决策本身，也分享决策背后的推理——会建立信任，并让各层级都能更好地自主决策。

Ultimately, effective communication in technical teams isn’t about perfection; it’s about creating an environment where misunderstandings are quickly identified and resolved. The best teams develop a shared language, establish explicit communication norms, and foster a culture where asking questions and seeking clarification are valued rather than penalized. With these foundations in place, even the most chaotic environments become navigable, enabling teams to collaborate effectively and deliver exceptional products.

说到底，技术团队里的有效沟通不在于完美；而在于营造一种环境，让误解能被迅速发现、迅速化解。最好的团队发展出共同语言、建立明确的沟通规范、培育一种“提问和寻求澄清受重视而非受惩罚”的文化。有了这些地基，即便是最混乱的环境也变得可以驾驭，让团队能高效协作、交付卓越的产品。

— 原书第 208 页 —

Exercise: The Architecture Telephone Game

练习：架构传话游戏

Finally, here’s an exercise we like that’s a fun activity focusing on communication, documentation, knowledge transfer, and technical precision. It’s also a pretty cool team-building exercise for an off-site. Follow these steps:

最后，介绍一个我们喜欢的练习——它好玩，又聚焦于沟通、文档、知识传递和技术精确性。它也是个相当不错的 off-site 团建活动。按以下步骤来做：

  1. Have your team sit in a circle, whether in person or virtually.

    让团队坐成一圈，线下或线上均可。

  2. Select a moderately complex system or feature that your team has built or is familiar with.

    选一个你们团队构建过、或熟悉的、中等复杂度的系统或功能。

  3. Select an initial participant. They draw (or better, use an existing diagram) a high-level architecture diagram of this system on paper or a digital whiteboard, visible only to them.

    选一位起始参与者。他在纸上或数字白板上画出（或更好——直接用一张现成的图）这个系统的高层架构图，只有他自己能看见。

  4. Select another person, and then, in another room or breakout room, the first participant has two minutes to verbally describe the architecture to the next person without showing them their diagram. This second person draws what they understand from the description.

    再选一个人，然后在另一个房间或分组讨论室里，第一位参与者有两分钟时间口头向对方描述这个架构，但不能展示自己的图。第二个人根据描述画出他所理解的内容。

  5. You then bring in a third person, and continue the process around the circle.

    然后你带上第三个人，沿着圆圈继续这个过程。

  6. After reaching the last person, compare everyone’s diagrams side by side. The differences between the first and last diagrams often reveal fascinating communication gaps and assumptions. Discuss specific moments where information was lost or transformed. Was it terminology differences, missing context, implicit knowledge that wasn’t stated, or something else?

    传到最后一个人之后，把所有人的图并排摆在一起比较。第一张和最后一张图之间的差异，往往会揭示出迷人的沟通缺口和默认假设。讨论那些信息丢失或被扭曲的具体时刻。是术语差异？缺失的上下文？没被说出来的隐含知识？还是别的什么？

The real value of this exercise comes in the debrief, where you identify patterns in how technical information degrades across transmission points. Teams who practice this regularly develop more precise technical vocabulary, learn to verify understanding through targeted questions, and become more aware of when they’re using jargon or making assumptions. Also, some of the final drawings are often pretty funny.

这个练习真正的价值在于复盘环节：你会识别出技术信息在一个个传递节点上是如何衰减的模式。经常练习的团队会发展出更精确的技术词汇，学会通过有针对性的问题来验证理解，并更清楚自己什么时候在用黑话、什么时候在做假设。此外，有些最后的画通常还挺好笑的。

Collaboration

协作

Cross-functional communication and collaboration aren’t just about having the right tools; it’s about creating a culture where different disciplines actively seek each other’s input and feedback. This requires deliberate effort to break down “us and them” mentalities that can develop between engineering, product, design, and other functions. Successful teams create opportunities for meaningful interaction, from informal coffee chats to structured cross-disciplinary pairing sessions.

跨职能的沟通与协作，不只是拥有合适的工具；更是营造一种文化，让不同学科主动寻求彼此的意见和反馈。这需要有意识地努力，去打破工程、产品、设计等职能之间可能滋生的“我们 vs 他们”心态。成功的团队会创造有意义互动的机会——从非正式的咖啡闲聊，到结构化的跨学科结对环节。

Effective cross-functional collaboration requires structural support. This might include tools, shared goals and metrics, cross-disciplinary habits like joint planning sessions, and leadership that rewards collaborative behaviors rather than siloed

有效的跨职能协作需要结构性支持。这可能包括工具、共享的目标与指标、联合规划会议之类的跨学科习惯，以及一种奖励协作行为、而非孤岛式

— 原书第 209 页 —

excellence. The goal isn’t to eliminate specialization but to ensure that specialists work together effectively toward common outcomes.

“单兵英雄主义”的领导力。目标不是消除专业化，而是确保专才们为共同的成果有效地协同工作。

Like bringing Slack conversations into open channels, the first step to collaboration is ensuring that everyone who needs to be involved in a decision or discussion is included and takes ownership of the outcome. If everyone has a stake in the outcome, then they are more likely to work together to resolve it. This also reduces the incidence of the “throw it over the wall” mentality.

就像把 Slack 对话搬到公开频道一样，协作的第一步是确保每个需要参与某项决策或讨论的人都被纳入进来，并对结果有主人翁感。如果每个人都在结果中有切身利害，他们就更可能一起去解决问题。这也减少了“把球扔过墙”那种心态的发生。

But breaking down this notorious mentality takes persistent effort. James once worked with a team where engineers built features exactly as specified, only to have them rejected by users. So, what was the root cause? Product managers were writing requirements without engineering input on feasibility, and engineers were implementing without asking clarifying questions. To solve this, James instituted kickoff sessions where product, engineering, and quality assurance teams collaboratively refined requirements before work began.

但要瓦解这种臭名昭著的心态，需要持久的努力。James 曾共事过一支团队，工程师们严格按规格造功能，结果却被用户拒之门外。根因是什么？产品经理写需求时没有征求工程侧对可行性的意见，工程师实现时也不问澄清性问题。为解决这个问题，James 设立了启动会，让产品、工程和质量保障团队在开工之前协作细化需求。

The physical (or virtual) environment has a massive impact on collaboration quality. Again, the default should be to open: have project and team channels where all parties can gather. Frequently, we see the engineering channel in Slack being private. Why? “So nonengineers don’t bug us” is usually the answer. Putting aside that engineers have jobs because people who bug them want things, those who ask in a public channel can be managed by not removing access to the public channel. Try directing people to a support channel instead of hiding your work from others.

物理（或虚拟）环境对协作质量有巨大影响。再说一遍，默认应该是开放的：设立项目和团队频道，让各方都能聚到一起。我们常看到 Slack 里的工程频道是私有的。为什么？答案通常是“这样非工程师就不会来烦我们”。先撇开“工程师之所以有工作，正是因为有人来烦他们、想做出东西”这一点不谈：那些在公开频道里提问的人，完全可以通过“不取消他们访问公开频道的权限”来管理。与其把你的工作对别人藏起来，不如试着把人引导到支持频道去。

Remote teams should be intentional about creating opportunities for serendipitous collaboration that might naturally occur in colocated environments. Some organizations implement virtual “office hours” where technical leaders or domain experts make themselves available for impromptu discussions and questions. Others create dedicated channels for specific technical domains or projects, encouraging ongoing discussion and ideation. These informal collaboration spaces complement more structured decision-making processes by enabling ideas to emerge and evolve through casual interaction before they are formalized into proposals.

远程团队应当有意识地去创造那些在同地办公环境里会自然发生的、不期而遇的协作机会。有些组织搞了虚拟的“办公时间”，让技术领导或领域专家在线，供大家即兴讨论和提问。另一些组织为特定技术领域或项目建专门频道，鼓励持续讨论和构思。这些非正式的协作空间，补充了更结构化的决策流程——让想法在被正式写成提案之前，先通过随意的互动涌现、演化。

Visual collaboration tools become critical for remote technical discussions that would traditionally happen at a whiteboard. Shared diagramming applications, digital Kanban boards, and collaborative documents enable distributed teams to create and manipulate shared representations of technical concepts in real-time or asynchronously. Teams that invest in building fluency with these tools and establishing norms around their use can maintain high-quality technical discussions despite physical distance. The most effective remote teams treat their virtual collaboration environment as a priority concern, continuously refining their tool choices and practices to support rich technical communication across distances.

对于那些传统上会在白板前发生的远程技术讨论，可视化协作工具变得至关重要。共享画图应用、数字看板、协作文档，让分布式团队能够实时或异步地创建和操作技术概念的共享表征。那些投入精力熟练掌握这些工具、并围绕其使用建立规范的团队，即便相隔千里也能维持高质量的技术讨论。最高效的远程团队把虚拟协作环境当作头等大事来对待，不断打磨工具选择和实践，以支持跨越距离的丰富技术沟通。

— 原书第 210 页 —

Shared language is also key for effective collaboration. When engineers talk about refactoring and technical debt, while product folk discuss user journeys and market fit, miscommunications are inevitable. This extends to explaining technical jargon and concepts to nontechnical audiences. Building a sense of empathy and understanding across functions will pay enormous dividends. Teams that understand each other’s challenges and constraints make better decisions together. Celebrating cross-functional wins specifically—not just team or individual achievements—reinforces collaborative behaviors.

共同的语言也是有效协作的关键。当工程师们在谈重构和技术债、产品同学在谈用户旅程和市场契合时，误解就在所难免。这还延伸到向非技术受众解释技术黑话和概念。在各职能之间建立共情与理解，会带来巨大回报。那些理解彼此挑战与约束的团队，能共同做出更好的决策。专门庆祝跨职能的胜利——而不只是团队或个人的成就——会强化协作行为。

Psychological safety becomes even more crucial in cross-functional settings. When people fear looking ignorant in front of colleagues from other disciplines, they won’t ask clarifying questions or offer alternative perspectives. One practice that works wonders is “designated novice” questions—having senior people deliberately ask basic questions that others might be afraid to voice. James worked with a senior engineer who used this technique regularly to tease out and encourage questions by asking, “Can you explain that concept again? I’m not following.” It created permission for everyone else to seek clarity without embarrassment.

在跨职能场合，心理安全变得更加关键。当人们害怕在其他学科的同事面前显得无知时，他们就不会问澄清性问题，也不会提出不同视角。有一个效果奇佳的做法是“指定新手”提问——让资深的人故意问那些别人可能不敢开口问的基础问题。James 曾共事过一位资深工程师，他经常用这招，通过问“你能再解释一下那个概念吗？我没跟上”来把问题逗引出来、鼓励大家提问。这让其他每个人都获得了许可，可以毫无尴尬地去寻求澄清。

There’s more on psychological safety in “Psychological Safety” on page 201.
关于心理安全的更多内容，见第 201 页“心理安全”一节。

Most importantly, true collaboration means sometimes changing direction based on input, not just collecting opinions and proceeding with your original plan. Nothing stifles the collaborative spirit faster than the perception that “my input never matters.” Openly acknowledging the value of that input and changing course creates a culture where people know that their expertise genuinely influences outcomes. This strengthens collaborative bonds for all future work.

最重要的是，真正的协作意味着有时要根据 input 改变方向，而不只是收集一圈意见后仍按原计划行事。没有什么比“我的意见从来无足轻重”这种感觉更扼杀协作精神的了。公开肯定那份意见的价值、并改变航向，会营造一种文化：让人们知道自己的专长真的能影响结果。这会为今后所有工作强化协作纽带。

Remember, collaboration isn’t some corporate feel-good exercise; it’s the practical recognition that complex products require diverse expertise working in concert. When engineers understand user needs, designers grasp technical constraints, and product folk appreciate implementation realities, that’s when the magic happens. The result isn’t just better products but more engaging work for everyone involved.

请记住，协作不是什么公司里的自我感觉良好的活动；它是一种务实的认识：复杂的产品需要多元的专长协同作战。当工程师理解用户需求、设计师把握技术约束、产品同学体会到实现的现实时，魔法才会发生。结果不只是更好的产品，也是让每个参与者都更投入的工作。

For James, at a large organization with many independent and remote teams, there were a lot of handovers from one team to the next: product to design, design to engineering, engineering to quality assurance. There was cognitive overhead in the handovers, and the teams frequently were not on the same page about requirements or timelines. James proposed a trial of cross-functional teams, and put everyone working on a specific product or feature in a single pod. Almost overnight, the level of collaboration soared. Instead of handovers, conversations happened in standups

对 James 来说，在一家有许多独立远程团队的大公司里，存在着大量团队之间的交接：产品交设计、设计交工程、工程交质量保障。这些交接带来了认知负担，各团队在需求或时间线上常常对不齐。James 提议试点跨职能团队，把为某个特定产品或功能工作的所有人放进同一个 pod（小组）里。几乎一夜之间，协作水平就飙升了。不再有交接，对话直接发生在站会上

— 原书第 211 页 —

and everyone had a clear picture of requirements and expectations. With collaboration came engagement, improved execution and delivery. It was a simple change with a big impact.

而且每个人对需求和预期都有了清晰的图景。随着协作而来的是投入度、更好的执行和交付。这是一个简单的改变，却带来了巨大的影响。

Execution

执行

Finally, there’s execution: the tasks and activities that make up day-to-day work for engineering teams. We’re going to touch on some of the key practices that, when done correctly, will pay dividends.

最后是执行：构成工程团队日常工作的那些任务和活动。我们会谈谈一些关键实践——做对了就会带来回报。

Effective coding practices

有效的编码实践

While technical principles provide high-level guidance, coding practices translate these principles into concrete, everyday behaviors. These practices cover everything from naming conventions and testing requirements to architectural patterns and documentation standards. They’re the practical manifestation of your principles; the “how” that supports the “why” of your technical vision.

技术原则提供的是高层指引，而编码实践把这些原则翻译成具体的、日常的行为。这些实践涵盖从命名约定、测试要求，到架构模式和文档标准的方方面面。它们是你的原则在实践中的体现；是支撑你技术愿景“为什么”的那个“怎么做”。

The most effective coding practices emerge collaboratively rather than being imposed from above. When engineers participate in defining standards, they’re more likely to follow them and advocate for their adoption across the team. This doesn’t mean decisions being made by a committee—someone still needs to make the final calls—but the process should incorporate diverse perspectives and experiences. Collaborative development of practices creates buy-in and ensures the standards address real problems the team faces rather than theoretical concerns or personal preferences of a single senior engineer.

最有效的编码实践是协作涌现出来的，而不是自上而下强加的。当工程师参与定义标准时，他们更可能去遵守、并在团队里推广。这并不意味着由委员会来做决策——总还是得有人拍板——但这个过程应当吸纳多元的视角和经验。协作式地制定实践会带来认同（buy-in），并确保这些标准针对的是团队真正面临的问题，而不是理论上的顾虑、或某一位资深工程师的个人偏好。

Consistency is the primary goal of coding practices. A consistent codebase is easier to understand, maintain, and extend, especially for new team members. But achieving consistency requires more than just writing down rules; it requires reinforcement through mentorship and review processes. Regular code reviews provide a powerful mechanism for enforcing coding practices while simultaneously serving as learning opportunities. When done well, they help disseminate knowledge throughout the team and elevate everyone’s skills. The key is approaching reviews with a spirit of collaboration rather than criticism, focusing on the code rather than the coder.

一致性是编码实践的首要目标。一致的代码库更容易理解、维护和扩展，对新人尤其如此。但要达成一致性，光把规则写下来还不够；还需要通过导师制和评审流程来强化。定期代码评审既是强制执行编码实践的有力机制，同时也是学习机会。做得好时，它们能把知识散播到整个团队，并提升每个人的水平。关键在于：以协作而非批评的精神来做评审，聚焦于代码而非写代码的人。

Like technical principles, coding practices should evolve with your team and technology. What works for a team of three might not work for a team of 30. Regular retrospectives can help identify which practices are adding value and which need refinement.

和技术原则一样，编码实践也应随团队和技术演进而演进。对三人团队有效的做法，对三十人的团队未必管用。定期复盘能帮你识别哪些实践在创造价值、哪些需要打磨。

Fortunately, you don’t need to create coding practices from scratch. Many open source projects and technology companies publicly share their standards, enabling you to steal—err—providing excellent starting points that you can adapt for your team.

幸运的是，你不必从零开始创造编码实践。许多开源项目和科技公司都公开分享了自己的标准，让你可以去“借鉴”——呃——为你提供极佳的起点，再针对自己的团队加以改造。

— 原书第 212 页 —

Navigating code-review drama

驾驭代码评审中的戏剧性场面

It’s important to directly and specifically call out code reviews. Before diving into the interpersonal dynamics of code reviews, it’s worth establishing why we do them at all. Code reviews serve multiple critical purposes: they catch bugs before they reach production, ensure code meets team standards, spread knowledge across the team, and provide mentorship opportunities. Most importantly, code reviews are about improving the collective output of the team, not gatekeeping or demonstrating superiority. When everyone understands that reviews exist to make the codebase better and help each other grow, the emotional temperature drops significantly. The goal isn’t to find fault; it’s to collaboratively ensure that what ships is maintainable, understandable, and aligned with your technical principles.

有必要专门、具体地把代码评审拎出来讲一讲。在钻进代码评审的人际动态之前，先值得说清楚我们到底为什么要做评审。代码评审有多个关键用途：在 bug 进入生产环境之前逮住它、确保代码符合团队标准、在团队间传播知识、以及提供导师指导的机会。最重要的是，代码评审是为了提升团队的集体产出，而不是为了设卡守门或炫耀优越感。当每个人都明白评审的存在是为了让代码库更好、帮助彼此成长，情绪温度就会显著下降。目标不是挑错；而是共同确保交付出去的东西可维护、可理解、并与你的技术原则对齐。

Code reviews can be tense if not handled carefully. Reviews that are too harsh can demoralize team members and create a culture of fear, while reviews that are too lenient can let quality issues slip through and accumulate technical debt. Finding the right balance requires empathy, clear expectations, and a shared understanding of the purpose of reviews.

代码评审处理不当就会变得剑拔弩张。过于严苛的评审会打击士气、制造恐惧文化；过于宽松的评审则会让质量问题溜过去、积累技术债。找到恰当的平衡需要共情、清晰的预期，以及对评审目的的共同理解。

Consider this common scenario: a junior engineer submits their first pull request, only to receive a barrage of critical comments from a senior engineer. Feeling discouraged, they approach another senior engineer, asking if they’re a terrible engineer who should quit. This situation requires addressing both immediate and systemic issues. In the short term, you need to reassure the junior engineer that critical feedback is part of the learning process, not a judgment of their worth. Help them understand that even experienced engineers receive substantial feedback on their code and that the review process is about improving the codebase, not criticizing the engineers.

想想这个常见场景：一位初级工程师提交了自己的第一个 Pull Request，结果收到一位资深工程师一连串的严厉批评。他倍感沮丧，跑去问另一位资深工程师：自己是不是个糟糕的工程师、该不干了。这种局面需要同时处理眼前问题和系统性问题。短期来看，你需要安抚这位初级工程师：批评性反馈是学习过程的一部分，不是对他个人价值的判决。帮他理解：即便是经验丰富的工程师，代码也会收到大量反馈；评审流程是为了改进代码库，而不是批评工程师本人。

In Practice: April’s Story

实践案例：April 的故事

April faced this exact scenario in her second week at PixelCurl. Emma, a junior engineer, submitted a pull request for a new API endpoint. Marcus left 47 comments, including gems like “This is wrong” and “Did you even read the documentation?” Emma went to April in tears, convinced she’s not cut out for engineering. So, April reviewed the pull request herself. She found that Emma’s code was actually solid, just not following Marcus’s personal preferences (which weren’t documented anywhere). April implemented a three-part solution. First, she created a code review checklist distinguishing “must fix” (security issues, bugs) from “consider” (style preferences). Second, she made it clear that tone matters; things can be critiqued but every critique must be constructive. Third, she paired Marcus with Emma for a week, instructing him to explain his standards in person. Marcus discovered that Emma has clever insights when not terrified, and Emma learned that the way Marcus critiques stems from caring about quality, not personal attacks.

April 在 PixelCurl 第二周就遇到了一模一样的场景。初级工程师 Emma 为一个新 API 端点提交了 PR。Marcus 留了 47 条评论，包括“这是错的”“你到底有没有读文档？”之类的金句。Emma 哭着去找 April，认定自己不是干工程的料。于是 April 自己去审了那个 PR。她发现 Emma 的代码其实挺扎实，只是不符合 Marcus 的个人偏好（而这些偏好哪儿都没写下来）。April 搞了个三步方案。第一，她做了一份代码评审清单，区分“必须改”（安全问题、bug）和“可考虑”（风格偏好）。第二，她明确语气很重要：可以批评，但每条批评都必须有建设性。第三，她让 Marcus 和 Emma 结对一周，要求他当面解释自己的标准。Marcus 发现 Emma 在不害怕的时候其实很有巧思；Emma 也明白了 Marcus 的批评方式源于对质量的在乎，而不是人身攻击。

— 原书第 213 页 —

At the same time, it’s important to speak privately with senior engineers who leave unempathetic comments and discuss how their feedback can be delivered constructively while still maintaining high standards. Emphasize that the goal of code reviews is to improve code quality and engineer growth, not to demonstrate superiority or catch mistakes. Many technical experts haven’t been taught how to provide effective feedback, and a conversation about review techniques and tone can be transformative. Suggest specific approaches, such as starting with positive observations before making suggestions, or framing comments as questions rather than directives.

与此同时，私下里和那些留下冷漠评论的资深工程师谈谈也很重要：讨论如何在维持高标准的同时，把反馈以有建设性的方式传递出去。要强调：代码评审的目标是提升代码质量和工程师的成长，不是展示优越感或挑错。许多技术专家从没被教过如何给出有效的反馈，一次关于评审技巧和语气的谈话可能带来转变。建议一些具体做法，比如先从正面观察说起再提建议，或把评论框定为问题而非指令。

This is a favorite interview technique that James uses with senior engineers. He asks them what they would do if approached by the junior engineer about what to do next after receiving a bad review. The answers tend to be deeply illuminating, especially when the answer is, “I’d tell them to suck it up because I learned the hard way too.”
这是 James 面试资深工程师时最爱用的一招。他会问：如果那位初级工程师在收到糟糕评审后跑来找你问下一步怎么办，你会怎么做？答案往往极具启发性——尤其是当答案是“我会告诉他忍忍吧，因为我当年也是这么苦过来的”的时候。

Systemically, this situation highlights the need for code review guidelines that establish expectations around tone, scope, and process. Some teams find it helpful to create templates that distinguish between must-fix issues and optional suggestions, or to establish norms like clearly defining appropriate language. James implemented a “code review buddies” system at a company, where junior engineers were paired with more experienced mentors who would review their code before the wider team reviewed it. This created a safer learning environment while still ensuring code quality. Over time, engineers naturally developed more constructive review habits, which fostered a better balance between thoroughness and empathy.

从系统层面看，这种局面凸显了代码评审指引的必要性——要在语气、范围和流程上建立预期。有些团队发现，创建模板来区分“必须改”和“可选建议”很有帮助；或建立诸如“明确界定得体用语”之类的规范。James 曾在一家公司推行“代码评审伙伴”制度：把初级工程师和更有经验的导师结对，导师先在更大范围评审之前看过他们的代码。这创造了更安全的学习环境，同时仍保证代码质量。久而久之，工程师们自然养成了更有建设性的评审习惯，在彻底性与共情之间达成了更好的平衡。

Making good technical decisions

做出好的技术决策

Those lofty technical principles we introduced earlier also come into play when we start thinking about making good technical decisions. Your principles guide how you make the decisions that turn strategic initiatives or goals into reality. But translating your principles into everyday practice requires some governance. Typically, in a massive enterprise, this involves setting up structures like an architecture governance board, whose job is to oversee all architectural initiatives and ensure they align with established principles. We can hear you yawning already, and we agree: boards like this are essentially committees powered by presentation slides. They are where ideas go to die, or worse, where awful ideas are given terrible life—much as Dr. Frankenstein created his monster. Instead, we like lean and mean alternatives, of which our favorite is the RFC.

我们前面引入的那些高远的技术原则，在开始思考如何做出好的技术决策时同样派上用场。你的原则指导你如何做决策，把战略举措或目标变为现实。但要把原则落到日常实践中，需要某种治理。通常，在一家巨型企业里，这意味着设立架构治理委员会之类的机构，其职责是监督所有架构举措、确保它们与既定原则对齐。我们已经能听见你打哈欠了——我们同意：这种委员会本质上就是一群靠演示幻灯片运转的委员会。它们是想法的葬身之地，或者更糟，是糟糕想法被糟糕地赋予生命的地方——就像弗兰肯斯坦博士造出他的怪物一样。相反，我们喜欢精简高效的替代方案，其中最爱的就是 RFC。

RFCs, or requests for comments, have been a common tool in engineering, especially when defining the standards for how the internet and internet-related protocols work. For example, RFC 822 is the original RFC that defines the structure of email messages. These are very formal documents that often take years to be reviewed

RFC（征求意见稿，request for comments）在工程界一直是常用工具，尤其是在定义互联网及相关协议如何运作的标准时。例如，RFC 822 就是定义电子邮件消息结构的原始 RFC。这些是非常正式的文档，往往要花好几年才能被评审

— 原书第 214 页 —

and approved. However, many projects and companies have stolen the name and elements of their structure to create fast and practical architecture documents that can detail technical, operational, and even cultural changes they want to document.

通过并批准。然而，许多项目和公司借用了这个名字和它的结构要素，创造出快速、实用的架构文档，用以详述他们想要记录的技术、运维乃至文化层面的变更。

So, what exactly does this new RFC species look like? Think of the modern RFC as your project’s blueprint, but friendlier; it’s a proposal that outlines significant changes or additions to your system. Imagine you’re planning to introduce a shiny new feature, use a fresh new tool, or maybe tweak the fundamental architecture of your beloved app. Instead of diving straight into code and risking chaos, you pause and write an RFC. This doesn’t just save you headaches; it actively invites your teammates into a thoughtful, structured discussion.

那么，这种新的 RFC 物种到底长什么样？把现代 RFC 想象成你项目的蓝图，但更友好一些；它是一份提案，概述对系统的重大变更或新增。想象你正打算引入一个闪亮的新功能、用一个全新的工具，或者微调一下你心爱应用的根本架构。与其一头扎进代码、冒着混乱的风险，不如停下来写一份 RFC。这不仅省得你头疼；它还主动邀请你的队友进入一场深思熟虑、结构化的讨论。

When you start using RFCs, you create a shared conversation space. Everyone can chime in: raising red flags, suggesting better solutions, or even offering a supportive thumbs-up. And here’s the magic: not only does this reduce nasty surprises later, but it also genuinely deepens the team’s shared knowledge. Have you ever worked somewhere where all the historical context lived only in someone’s head? RFCs help avoid precisely that. By writing things down, you help everyone—current and future teammates—get up to speed effortlessly.

当你开始用 RFC，你就创造了一个共享的对话空间。每个人都能插上一嘴：亮出红旗、提出更好的方案、甚至点个赞表示支持。魔法在于：这不仅减少了日后的恶心意外，还真正深化了团队的共享知识。你有没有在那种“所有历史背景都只存在某个人脑子里”的地方待过？RFC 恰恰帮你避免这种情况。把事情写下来，你就帮所有人——现在和未来的队友——毫不费力地跟上了进度。

That shared conversation has guidelines, too: your technical principles. Our first step in reviewing any RFC is to validate that it aligns with our principles quickly. This is why the first example of a principle we posited is about simplicity. If you find yourself reading an RFC that seems like a maze of twisty passages, you’re likely reading something too complex. Issues with other principles will also become readily apparent: modularity, maintainability, and scalability are all easy to determine when reviewing RFCs.

那场共享对话也有自己的指引：你的技术原则。我们评审任何 RFC 的第一步，就是快速验证它是否与我们的原则对齐。这就是为什么我们提出的第一条原则是关于简洁的。如果你读一份 RFC 读得像一座曲折通道的迷宫，那它很可能过于复杂了。与其他原则相关的问题也会 readily 显现出来：在评审 RFC 时，模块化、可维护性、可扩展性都很容易判断。

Many teams adopt RFCs because they want more explicit ownership and fewer of the surprise design-by-committee meetings. Almost everywhere that we’ve seen or introduced RFCs, we’ve seen an acceleration in the time it takes to make technical decisions. Before RFCs, decisions often dragged on without clear direction, ending in endless meetings and frustrating bikeshedding. After implementing a straightforward RFC process, the team could suddenly say, “This idea belongs to Ana,” or “Jamal owns this decision.” Clear ownership meant faster, bolder moves without the fear of failure looming. People felt freer to take smart risks because they knew the team had considered potential pitfalls.
