许多团队采用 RFC，是因为他们想要更明确的权责、更少那种突如其来的“委员会式设计”会议。几乎在我们见过或引入 RFC 的每一个地方，做技术决策的时间都缩短了。在 RFC 之前，决策常常拖拖拉拉、方向不明，最后变成没完没了的会议和令人沮丧的“自行车棚效应”（在琐事上争论不休）。实施了一套直截了当的RFC 流程之后，团队突然就能说：“这个想法归 Ana”，或“这个决策 Jamal 说了算”。清晰的权责意味着更快、更大胆的行动，而不必被失败的阴云笼罩。人们更敢于去冒聪明的风险，因为他们知道团队已经考虑过潜在的坑。

In Practice: April’s Story

实践案例：April 的故事

Before April introduced RFCs in the studio operations team, technical decisions happened through “whoever builds it first, wins.” This led to their current mess: three different logging systems because each senior engineer started building before discussing alternatives. April’s first RFC requirement seemed simple: “Any new tool or pattern

在 April 把 RFC 引入工作室运营团队之前，技术决策靠的是“谁先建完谁赢”。这就造成了他们如今的烂摊子：三套不同的日志系统，因为每位资深工程师都没讨论替代方案就开建了。April 的第一条 RFC 要求看似简单：“任何新工具或新模式

— 原书第 215 页 —

requires an RFC.” So, Marcus immediately tested this with an RFC proposing to rewrite the entire backend in Rust. But the RFC process worked exactly as intended: Sarah pointed out they’d need to hire three Rust developers (market rate: $300k each), and Derek calculated that the rewrite would take 18 months during which no features would ship. In addition, the juniors asked how this helped the company’s immediate goal of shipping the 4K rendering feature. Marcus withdrew the RFC and submitted a new one: “Optimize hot paths in existing Node.js backend, ” which was approved and delivered a three-times performance improvement in three weeks.

都需要一份 RFC。”于是 Marcus 立刻拿这个来试了一把：提了一份用 Rust 重写整个后端的RFC。但 RFC 流程恰如其分地起了作用：Sarah 指出他们得招三位 Rust 开发者（市场价：每人 30 万美元）；Derek 算了一下，重写要花 18 个月，其间一个功能都发不出去。此外，初级工程师们问：这跟公司眼下要交付4K 渲染功能的目标有什么关系？Marcus 撤回了那份 RFC，重新提交了一份：“优化现有 Node.js 后端的热路径”——这份获批了，并在三周内带来了三倍的性能提升。

Here’s how an RFC process typically looks: when you have an idea, you fill out a structured but simple template. Outline what you’re proposing, why it’s beneficial, possible drawbacks, and what alternative approaches you considered. Engage with the following example of an RFC template filled out to define the RFC for RFCs (yes, there are turtles all the way down) that helps explain how the workflow works in most organizations we’ve led.

RFC 流程通常长这样：当你有个想法时，填一份结构化但简单的模板。写清楚你提议什么、为什么有益、可能的缺点、以及你考虑过哪些替代方案。请看下面这份填好的 RFC 模板示例——它定义的是“关于 RFC 的 RFC”（没错，这一路都是乌龟，层层嵌套）——它能帮你理解我们所领导过的大多数组织里这个流程是怎么跑的。

Example: A Real-World RFC

示例：一份真实的 RFC

This example shows an RFC about implementing the RFC process itself, which demonstrates the structure and approach while providing a meta-example of the process in action:

这个示例展示的是一份关于“实施 RFC 流程本身”的 RFC，它在演示结构与方法的同时，也提供了一个流程正在运转的元示例：

Title: RFC on RFCs

标题：关于 RFC 的 RFC

Main Author: @buritica

主要作者：@buritica

Backers: @kartar

支持者：@kartar

Status: Draft, in review, rejected, approved

状态：草稿、评审中、已拒绝、已批准

Summary: This proposal will structure how the [redacted] team makes technical decisions.

摘要：本提案将规范 [已隐去] 团队如何做出技术决策。

Motivation: By formalizing a technical decision process, we become a more effective and efficient team by enabling the following:

动机：通过把技术决策流程正式化，我们将变得更有效、更高效，具体体现在：

— 原书第 216 页 —

  • Add a light, early stage of technical design that helps us understand our goals and evaluate decisions before writing heavy implementations.

    增加一个轻量的早期技术设计阶段，帮我们在动手写重实现之前先理解目标、评估决策。

  • Create opportunities to raise risks or concerns based on our shared experience. One of us may have solved a similar problem before, but belong to a different team. This process enables us to share our expertise and past mistakes.

    创造机会，让大家基于共同经验提出风险或顾虑。我们中可能有人以前解决过类似问题，只是在另一个团队。这个流程让我们能分享专长和过去犯过的错。

  • Sharing institutional knowledge by exposing the entire team to different domain problems will improve the shared understanding of our platform.

    通过让整个团队接触不同领域的问题来分享组织知识，将增进大家对我们平台的共同理解。

  • Centralize initial design documentation.

    把初始设计文档集中管理。

  • Facilitate the future onboarding of new members, as they will be able to dive into the context of how we made certain decisions in the past.

    便利未来新成员的入职，让他们能够深入了解我们过去做某些决策时的背景。

  • Update documentation by treating RFCs as live documents when past decisions need to be updated due to new information or features.

    当过去的决策因新信息或新功能而需要更新时，把 RFC 当作活文档来更新文档。

  • Establish a shared sense of belonging by including our team in the process of important decisions.

    通过让团队参与重要决策的过程，建立共同的归属感。

  • Diminished fear of failure by having a process where critical technical risks are identified. This will enable us to make bolder approaches as a team.

    通过建立一个识别关键技术风险的流程，减少对失败的恐惧。这将让我们作为一个团队敢于采取更大胆的做法。

  • Establish clear ownership. By enabling individuals and teams to propose and make critical decisions, we can take calculated risks, make mistakes, and enable continuous improvement.

    建立清晰的权责。让个人和团队能够提出并做出关键决策，我们就能冒经过计算的风险、犯错，并实现持续改进。

  • Encourage constant learning, by allowing members of diverse backgrounds to provide input.

    通过让不同背景的成员提供意见，鼓励持续学习。

  • Gain clarity in the decision-making process by guaranteeing that those responsible for the decisions are leading the process, preventing bikeshedding, and reducing design-by-committee and brainstorming sessions.

    让决策过程更清晰：确保对决策负责的人主导流程，防止自行车棚效应，减少委员会式设计和头脑风暴会议。

Detailed Design: When to RFC. The distinction between when to create an RFC and when not to is not always clear. Engineers are expected to use good judgment when determining whether an RFC is necessary. Minor updates to endpoints may not require an RFC, but when in doubt, ask [redacted] whether specific work requires a proposal.

详细设计：什么时候该写 RFC。什么时候该写、什么时候不该写 RFC，界限并不总是清晰。需要工程师运用良好的判断力来决定是否有必要写 RFC。对端点的小改动可能不需要 RFC；但拿不准时，就去问[已隐去] 某项具体工作是否需要提案。

The following are some guidelines that may be used to determine whether a proposal is needed (though note that the cases do not always mandate a proposal):

以下是一些可用于判断是否需要提案的指引（但请注意，列举的情形并不总是强制要求写提案）：

  • Will a new feature require a new endpoint?

    新功能是否需要一个新端点？

  • Are you starting a new project?

    你是否在启动一个新项目？

  • Will your changes have an architectural impact?

    你的改动是否会产生架构层面的影响？

  • Are you proposing using a new tool, library, technology, or process?

    你是否在提议使用新工具、新库、新技术或新流程？

— 原书第 217 页 —

RFCs may not be part of the initial process only. Sometimes, teammates may request a proposal to justify or argue modifications in an existing pull request—for example, when a new dependency is added to a system or a proposed modification has a broader system impact than initially expected.

RFC 并不只在最初的流程中才出现。有时，队友可能会要求一份提案，来论证或争辩对某个已有 Pull Request 的修改——例如，当系统新增了一个依赖、或某项拟议改动对系统的影响比最初预期更大时。

Detailed Design: How to RFC. For new proposals, follow these steps:

详细设计：怎么写 RFC。对于新提案，遵循以下步骤：

  1. Create an RFC template. One of the superpowers of RFCs is the consistency of their design, encouraging requests to consider different concepts with equal criteria.

    创建一份 RFC 模板。RFC 的超能力之一就是其设计的一致性，促使各类请求按统一标准来考量不同的概念。

  2. Clone and fill that template in a new branch of a repository, create a Notion page, or manage your RFCs however you like.

    在仓库的新分支里克隆并填写该模板、建一个 Notion 页面，或随你喜欢的方式管理你的 RFC。

  • We like prefixing a numbered 000X so we can track RFCs.

    我们喜欢加一个编号前缀 000X，以便追踪 RFC。

  • You may want to label an RFC in process with a WIP tag or title.

    你可能想给进行中的 RFC 打个 WIP 标签或在标题里标注。

  1. When ready for comments, open your pull request or share your RFC with your team.

    准备好征求意见后，开你的 Pull Request，或把 RFC 分享给团队。

  2. Send a calendar invitation:

    发一份日历邀请：

  • To: [redacted]

    收件人：[已隐去]

  • Title: [RFC] 000X deadline

    标题：[RFC] 000X 截止日期

  • All day event: Yes (marked as free)

    全天事件：是（标记为空闲）

  • Alert: on the day of the event

    提醒：事件当天

  • Description: link to RFC

    描述：RFC 链接

  1. All members of [redacted] are expected to read and add comments to the pull request or document within the expected timeframe. Members may indicate they’ve read the document and have no comments; votes are not required.

    [已隐去] 的所有成员都应在预期时间内阅读 PR 或文档并添加评论。成员可以表明自己已读过文档、没有评论；不需要投票。

  2. The author(s) and backers should resolve necessary comments and indicate which suggestions will not be addressed according to their judgment.

    作者和支持者应处理必要的评论，并根据自己的判断说明哪些建议不会被采纳。

  3. [Redacted] will approve by merging the pull request or marking the RFC as approved or vetoed, or may delegate someone for approval.

Next steps

后续步骤

From the example, you can see that the format is straightforward but comprehensive. Then, once your RFC is ready for review, like many open source projects, it can become a pull request. In other organizations, they could be centralized in tools like Notion or internal wikis. Teammates then read it, drop comments, ask questions, or just mark that they’ve reviewed it. Then, after some healthy debate, the decision makers merge it in or approve it. And voilà—RFC becomes official documentation, clearly capturing why certain decisions were made.

从这个示例你可以看到，格式直截了当却又面面俱到。然后，一旦 RFC 准备好评审，像许多开源项目一样，它可以变成一个 Pull Request。在另一些组织里，它们可以集中放在 Notion 或内部 wiki 之类的工具中。队友们随后阅读它、留下评论、提出问题，或只是标记一下自己已经评审过。然后，经过一番健康的辩论，决策者把它合并或批准。瞧——RFC 就成了正式文档，清楚地记录下某些决策当初为什么那么做。

RFCs are also living documents. They evolve as your project grows. If you’ve got new insights or changes that invalidate an old decision, then update the RFC! This fluidity makes RFCs incredibly valuable for maintaining an up-to-date narrative of your project’s evolution. A good RFC process doesn’t lock people out but invites them in. By sharing readable versions of RFCs, you can integrate nontechnical stakeholders. This keeps the whole organization in sync, not just the engineering crew.

RFC 还是活文档。它们随项目成长而演进。如果你有了新的洞见、或新的变化使某个旧决策不再成立，那就更新RFC！这种流动性让 RFC 在维护项目演进的最新叙事方面极具价值。一套好的 RFC 流程不是把人挡在门外，而是邀请他们进来。通过分享 RFC 的可读版本，你可以把非技术干系人也整合进来。这让整个组织——而不只是工程团队——保持同步。

What about architecture decision records?

那架构决策记录呢？

You’ve probably also heard about architecture decision records or ADRs. We think they’re worth mentioning as another form of technical architecture documentation. While RFCs help teams make decisions collaboratively before implementation, ADRs serve as the historical record of decisions already made. Think of RFCs as prospective decision-making tools and ADRs as retrospective decision documentation. Both are essential components of a comprehensive technical decision framework.

你大概也听说过架构决策记录（ADR）。我们认为它值得一提，是技术架构文档的另一种形式。RFC 帮助团队在实现之前协作做出决策，而 ADR 则是已经做出的决策的历史记录。把 RFC 想成前瞻性的决策工具，把 ADR 想成回顾性的决策文档。两者都是一套完整技术决策框架中不可或缺的组成部分。

ADRs capture the context, decision, and consequences of architectural choices in a lightweight, standardized format. Unlike RFCs, which invite discussion and debate, ADRs document decisions that are final, providing future team members with the reasoning behind past choices. A typical ADR includes the problem context, considered options, the chosen solution, and expected consequences—both positive and negative.

ADR 以一种轻量、标准化的格式，记录架构选择的背景、决策和后果。RFC 邀请讨论和辩论，ADR 则不同，它记录的是已经最终敲定的决策，为未来的团队成员提供过去那些选择背后的推理。一份典型的 ADR 包括：问题背景、考虑过的选项、选定的方案、以及预期的后果——好的和坏的。

The relationship between RFCs and ADRs creates a powerful decision lifecycle. An RFC might propose introducing microservices to solve scalability challenges, gather team input, and iterate through multiple revisions. Once approved and implemented, an ADR would document the final decision: “We chose to decompose our monolith into microservices to improve team autonomy and system scalability, accepting the trade-offs of increased operational complexity and network latency.”

RFC 与 ADR 之间的关系创造了一个强大的决策生命周期。一份 RFC 可能提议引入微服务来解决可扩展性挑战，收集团队意见，经过多轮修订迭代。一旦批准并实现，一份 ADR 会记录下最终决策：“我们选择把单体拆解为微服务，以提升团队自主性和系统可扩展性，同时接受运维复杂度上升和网络延迟增加这些权衡。”

Many teams find value in automatically generating ADRs from approved RFCs, ensuring that decisions don’t get lost in implementation details. Some organizations even reference specific ADRs in their RFCs, building on previous decisions and creating a connected web of architectural reasoning.

许多团队发现，从已批准的 RFC 自动生成 ADR 很有价值，能确保决策不会迷失在实现细节里。有些组织甚至在RFC 里引用特定的 ADR，在过去决策的基础上继续构建，织就一张相互连接的架构推理之网。

— 原书第 220 页 —

The key distinction: use RFCs when you need collaborative input on what to do, and ADRs to record what you actually did and why. Together, they create a comprehensive decision audit trail that prevents teams from repeatedly relitigating settled questions or forgetting the hard-won lessons from previous architectural choices.

关键区别是：当你需要就“做什么”征集协作意见时用 RFC；用 ADR 记录你实际做了什么、以及为什么。两者合在一起，构成了一条完整的决策审计轨迹，防止团队反复重提已经定论的问题，或忘记从以往架构选择中辛苦换来的教训。

You can find some excellent ADR resources and examples in the GitHub repository by Joel Parker Henderson.
你可以在 Joel Parker Henderson 的 GitHub 仓库里找到一些极佳的 ADR 资源和示例。

Leadership

领导力

Finally, we’ve discussed leaders’ modeling behaviors frequently throughout the book: this applies to all aspects of communication, collaboration, and execution. And beyond modeling behaviors, leaders create the conditions for the success of all these aspects through their decisions on how they spend their time. When they dedicate time to code reviews, technical discussions, and knowledge sharing, they signal that these activities are valued. When they protect teams from constant context switching and unrealistic deadlines, they create space for thoughtful decision making rather than reactive firefighting. By aligning incentives with collaborative behaviors, recognizing team achievements, celebrating knowledge sharing, and rewarding cross-functional problem-solving, they build organizational cultures where quality software is built and shipped effectively.

最后，我们在全书里反复谈到领导者要以身作则：这一点适用于沟通、协作和执行的方方面面。而除了以身作则之外，领导者还通过自己如何分配时间的决策，为这一切的成功创造条件。当他们把时间投入代码评审、技术讨论和知识分享时，他们是在发出信号：这些活动是受重视的。当他们保护团队免于无休止的上下文切换和不切实际的截止日期时，他们为深思熟虑的决策、而非被动救火，创造了空间。通过让激励与协作行为对齐、表彰团队成就、庆祝知识分享、奖励跨职能的问题解决，他们构建起一种能高效构建并交付高质量软件的组织文化。

Decision Making in Chaotic Conditions

混沌条件下的决策

All of these communication, collaboration, and execution steps require making a lot of decisions. In chaotic environments, the ability to make quick decisions is key. We want to streamline processes for reversible decisions, enabling teams to act swiftly without unnecessary debate. We also want to concentrate efforts on irreversible, higher-stake decisions and to spend time more effectively and reduce decision fatigue among team members. Effective decision making in chaotic conditions hinges on a blend of emotional intelligence, clear communication, and collaboration. To create the potential for this, we need to create an environment in which all of this can flourish.

所有这些沟通、协作和执行的环节，都需要做出大量决策。在混乱的环境里，快速决策的能力是关键。我们希望为可逆的决策简化流程，让团队不必经过无谓辩论就能迅速行动。我们也希望把精力集中在不可逆、高利害的决策上，更有效地投入时间，并减少团队成员的决策疲劳。混沌条件下的有效决策，取决于情商、清晰沟通与协作三者的融合。要让这一切成为可能，我们需要营造一个让它们都能蓬勃生长的环境。

Psychological Safety

心理安全

Psychological safety is the belief that one won’t be punished or humiliated for speaking up, and it is the foundation of effective collaborative decision making. Teams where members feel safe to share half-formed ideas, raise concerns, or admit mistakes make better decisions because they have access to more complete information and diverse perspectives. This safety isn’t about avoiding critique or lowering

心理安全，是指一个人相信自己开口说话不会受到惩罚或羞辱；它是有效协作决策的基石。在成员敢于分享尚不成熟的想法、提出顾虑、或承认错误的团队里，决策会更好，因为他们能接触到更完整的信息和多元的视角。这种安全不是为了回避批评或降低

— 原书第 221 页 —

standards; it’s about creating an environment where the focus is on improving work rather than judging people. James worked with a team where the chief technology officer (CTO) had a habit of immediately shooting down ideas he disagreed with. Over time, engineers stopped proposing innovative solutions and instead defaulted to approaches that they knew the CTO would approve. The outcomes were a poorer quality of solution and a culture that was rife with low morale and lack of enthusiasm—and, in turn, high turnover and lack of interest in the technical outcomes.

标准；而是营造一种环境，让焦点放在改进工作上，而不是评判人。James 曾共事过一支团队，其首席技术官（CTO）习惯一听到自己不认同的想法就当场毙掉。久而久之，工程师们不再提出创新方案，而是默认选择那些他们知道 CTO 会批准的做法。结果是：方案质量更差，文化里弥漫着低落士气和缺乏热情——进而导致高离职率、对技术结果漠不关心。

In Practice: April’s Story

实践案例：April 的故事

April inherited a similar dynamic in the studio operations team, but it was peer driven. In architecture meetings, whoever spoke the loudest would win—usually Marcus. Sarah stopped proposing frontend improvements after Marcus called React Hooks “trendy garbage.” Derek only spoke when directly asked for input, and the juniors didn’t speak at all. So, April restructured these meetings: everyone wrote their proposals on sticky notes first (virtual or physical), and then discussed. Attempts to shut down discussion on bogus grounds were quashed by April. Suddenly, quiet Derek’s suggestion to use database connection pooling saved $3,000 a month in AWS costs. Junior engineer Alex proposed a caching strategy that reduced API latency by 60%. Sarah felt safe enough to admit she didn’t understand Derek’s database indexes, leading to a knowledge-sharing session that helped everyone. Within a month, meeting participation went from three speakers to eight, and the quality of technical decisions improved dramatically.

April 在工作室运营团队接手了类似的动态，但那是同事之间互相造成的。在架构会议上，谁喊得最响谁就赢——通常是 Marcus。在 Marcus 把 React Hooks 称为“赶时髦的垃圾”之后，Sarah 就不再提前端改进了。Derek 只在被直接点名征求意见时才开口，初级工程师们则根本不说话。于是 April 重组了这些会议：每个人先把自己的提案写在便签上（虚拟或实体），然后再讨论。有人想拿莫须有的理由掐断讨论，都会被April 压下去。结果，一向沉默的 Derek 提出使用数据库连接池，每月省下了 3000 美元的 AWS 开销；初级工程师 Alex 提出了一套缓存策略，把 API 延迟降低了 60%；Sarah 终于敢承认自己看不懂 Derek 的数据库索引，由此引发了一场帮到所有人的知识分享。一个月之内，会议发言者从三个人增加到八个人，技术决策的质量也大幅提升。

Building psychological safety requires consistent, deliberate action from leaders. It means acknowledging your own mistakes openly, showing genuine curiosity about others’ perspectives, and responding constructively to bad news. When you react to a production incident by asking “What can we learn?” rather than “Who screwed up?”, you send a message about the team’s values. Similarly, when you explicitly welcome dissenting opinions during decision-making processes and thank people for raising concerns, you create space for honest communication that is essential for effective decision making.

建立心理安全，需要领导者持续而有意识的行动。它意味着公开承认自己的错误、对他人的视角展现真正的好奇、并对坏消息做出建设性的回应。当你面对一次生产事故时问的是“我们能学到什么？”而不是“是谁搞砸了？”，你就在传递团队的价值观。同样，当你在决策过程中明确欢迎不同意见、并感谢人们提出顾虑时，你就为坦诚沟通创造了空间——而坦诚沟通对有效决策至关重要。

The benefits of psychological safety extend beyond better technical decisions to increased innovation, faster problem-solving, and higher retention. When team members feel safe taking interpersonal risks, they are more likely to share creative ideas, flag potential issues early, and invest in the team’s success. They spend less energy on self-protection and more on solving problems collaboratively. Over time, this creates a virtuous cycle where trust begets more trust, and the team’s ability to tackle complex challenges together grows stronger with each interaction.

心理安全的好处不止于更好的技术决策，还包括更多的创新、更快的问题解决和更高的留任率。当团队成员敢于承担人际风险时，他们更可能分享创造性想法、尽早指出潜在问题、并为团队的成功投入。他们把更少的精力花在自我保护上，更多地花在协作解决问题上。久而久之，这会形成一个良性循环：信任催生更多信任，团队共同应对复杂挑战的能力随每一次互动而增强。

— 原书第 222 页 —

Inclusive and Data-Driven Decision Making

包容且数据驱动的决策

Technical decision making is where principles and practices converge with the messy reality of competing priorities, tight deadlines, and limited information. The most effective technical decisions strike a balance between data-driven analysis and inclusive input from the team. While RFCs and other structured processes provide valuable frameworks, they’re effective only when they genuinely include all relevant perspectives. Technical decisions often impact not just engineers but also product managers, designers, site reliability engineering (SRE) or operations teams, and other stakeholders. Inclusive decision making ensures these diverse viewpoints are considered, leading to more robust solutions and stronger alignment.

技术决策，是原则与实践同“相互竞争的优先级、紧迫的截止日期、有限的信息”这团乱麻现实交汇的地方。最有效的技术决策，在数据驱动的分析与团队的包容式 input 之间取得平衡。虽然 RFC 和其他结构化流程提供了宝贵的框架，但只有当它们真正纳入所有相关视角时才有效。技术决策影响的往往不只是工程师，还有产品经理、设计师、站点可靠性工程（SRE）或运维团队、以及其他干系人。包容式决策确保这些多元视角都被考虑到，从而带来更稳健的方案和更强的对齐。

This can go too far as well. So, like all good things, do it in moderation. Think carefully about who to invite, and adjust based on feedback. We’ve all been invited to a meeting that we didn’t need to be at. Good meeting etiquette, like having an “it’s okay to vote with your feet and leave a meeting that you’re not adding value to” is also useful here.
这件事也可能做过头。所以像所有好事一样，要适度。仔细想想该请谁，并根据反馈调整。我们都被请去过那种自己根本不需要参加的会。好的会议礼仪在这里也管用——比如“你可以用脚投票，离开一个你提供不了价值的会”。

A common challenge is making technical discussions accessible to nontechnical participants. This doesn’t mean simplifying complex topics, but instead focusing on outcomes and implications rather than implementation details when communicating across disciplines. Inclusive decision making also means considering diverse technical perspectives too. Junior engineers often hesitate to contribute to discussions dominated by senior voices, yet they can offer fresh perspectives unconstrained by “the way things have always been done.” Different perspectives can uncover gaps in understanding and generate creative solutions that no individual would discover alone. This doesn’t mean everyone gets an equal vote, but it does mean creating opportunities for all voices to be heard.

一个常见的挑战是：如何让技术讨论对非技术参与者也友好。这不是要把复杂的话题简单化，而是在跨学科沟通时聚焦于结果和影响、而非实现细节。包容式决策也意味着同时考虑多元的技术视角。初级工程师往往怯于在被资深声音主导的讨论中发言，但他们能提供不受“一贯做法”束缚的新鲜视角。不同的视角能揭示理解上的缺口，激发出任何单个人都想不到的创造性方案。这并不意味着每个人都有平等的投票权，但确实意味着要为所有声音被听到创造机会。

Transparency around decisions also strengthens inclusive decision making. When team members understand how and why decisions are made, they are more likely to accept outcomes, even when they disagree with them. Explicitly stating the factors being considered—such as technical merit, resource constraints, and business priorities—helps align expectations and reduce friction. It also helps team members grow and develop: if they want to progress professionally they need to understand how these components interact in making a team function.

决策的透明性也会强化包容式决策。当团队成员理解决策是如何、以及为何做出时，他们更可能接受结果——即便自己并不认同。明确说出正在考量的因素——比如技术优劣、资源约束、业务优先级——有助于对齐预期、减少摩擦。它还有助于团队成员成长：如果他们想在职业上进步，就需要理解这些要素是如何相互作用、让团队运转起来的。

Finally, use data. Whenever possible, back your decisions with data. Data helps eliminate personal biases and provides objective criteria for evaluating options. However, in chaotic environments, perfect data is rarely available. When you can’t get comprehensive data up front, build proof-of-concept implementations or small experiments to gather empirical evidence. This approach lets you test hypotheses with minimal investment before making bigger commitments.

最后，用数据。只要可能，就用数据支撑你的决策。数据有助于消除个人偏见，为评估选项提供客观标准。然而在混乱环境里，完美的数据几乎总是拿不到。当你无法事先获得全面数据时，就构建概念验证实现或小型实验来收集实证证据。这种做法让你在做出更大承诺之前，以最小的投入检验假设。

— 原书第 223 页 —

Continuous Improvement

持续改进

Like all aspects of software development, collaborative decision processes benefit from regular reflection and refinement. Periodically reviewing the effectiveness of your RFC process, code review practices, or other collaborative mechanisms helps identify opportunities for improvement and keep these processes aligned with your team’s evolving needs.

和软件开发的所有方面一样，协作决策流程也受益于定期反思和打磨。周期性地检视 RFC 流程、代码评审实践或其他协作机制的有效性，有助于发现改进机会，并让这些流程与团队不断演进的需求保持对齐。

Post-decision retrospectives can be particularly valuable. After implementing a significant technical decision, gather the team to discuss what went well in the decision process, what could have been improved, and what lessons should inform future decisions.

决策之后的复盘可能尤其有价值。在实施了一项重大技术决策之后，把团队聚到一起讨论：决策过程中哪些做得好、哪些本可以改进、以及哪些教训应当指导未来的决策。

Continuous improvement isn’t just about fixing problems; it’s also about amplifying what works well. When teams identify effective practices, they can formalize and spread them throughout the organization. For example, a particularly successful approach to requirements gathering in one team might become a template shared across the company. Similarly, metrics that prove helpful in evaluating one type of decision might be adapted for other contexts. This positive reinforcement cycle helps build a culture of learning and adaptation, where teams constantly refine their approach based on real-world experience.

持续改进不只是修问题；也是把行之有效的做法放大。当团队识别出有效的实践，就可以把它固化下来、推广到整个组织。例如，某个团队里一种特别成功的需求收集方式，可能成为全公司共享的模板。同样，被证明有助于评估某类决策的指标，也可能被改造后用于其他场景。这种正向强化的循环有助于建立学习与适应的文化，让团队基于真实世界的经验不断打磨自己的做法。

The most successful teams recognize that their decision processes shouldn’t remain static as their context evolves. As teams grow, technologies change, and business priorities shift, the processes that served them well previously may need adjustment. Regular check-ins specifically focused on process health—separate from project-specific retrospectives—provide space to examine these broader patterns and make intentional changes. By treating their decision frameworks as products worthy of ongoing refinement rather than fixed rules, teams can maintain the right balance of structure and flexibility to navigate an ever-changing technical landscape.

最成功的团队认识到：随着情境演进，他们的决策流程不应一成不变。随着团队成长、技术变迁、业务优先级转移，过去很好用的流程可能需要调整。专门聚焦流程健康度的定期检查——与项目-specific 的复盘分开——提供了空间来审视这些更宏观的模式、并做出有意识的改变。把决策框架当作值得持续打磨的产品、而非固定规则，团队就能在结构与灵活之间保持恰当平衡，以驾驭不断变化的技术版图。

Finally, as leaders, we play a crucial role in improving how the team makes good decisions. This doesn’t mean making all decisions ourselves—quite the opposite. Not only is that counterproductive, but it’s a fast path to burnout. Effective leaders create environments where good decisions emerge from well-structured processes and empowered teams, guiding without micromanagement. It’s important to remember, though, that leaders are always still accountable for the decisions that are being made.

最后，作为领导者，我们在改进团队如何做好决策方面扮演关键角色。这不意味着所有决策都由我们自己来做——恰恰相反。那不仅适得其反，还是通往 burnout 的快车道。高效的领导者营造这样的环境：好的决策从结构良好的流程和被赋能的团队中涌现，他们引导而不微观管理。但重要的是要记住：领导者始终要对正在做出的决策负责。

In Practice: April’s Story

实践案例：April 的故事

Three months into April’s RFC process in the studio operations team, they ran their first retrospective on the process itself. The findings were illuminating: RFCs under two pages got quick approval, but anything longer stalled. Marcus admitted that he didn’t read past page 3. Sarah pointed out that synchronous RFC reviews in meetings ate up too much time. The juniors hesitated to comment on senior engineers’ RFCs, fearing they would

在工作室运营团队推行 RFC 流程三个月后，他们针对这个流程本身做了第一次复盘。发现很有启发性：两页以内的 RFC 很快获批，但凡超过两页就卡住。Marcus 承认他读不过第三页。Sarah 指出在会议上同步评审 RFC 太耗时间。初级工程师们不敢对资深工程师的 RFC 留言，害怕自己会

— 原书第 224 页 —

look stupid. April iterated: RFCs now have a strict two-page limit with appendices for details. Reviews became asynchronous-first, with optional discussion meetings. They also added an “RFC buddy” system where juniors are explicitly assigned to review and must ask at least one question (removing the fear of whether they “should” comment). The refined process cut decision time from two weeks to three days while improving decision quality through more diverse input.

显得很蠢。April 做了迭代：现在 RFC 严格限两页，细节放附录。评审改为异步优先，讨论会议可选。他们还加了一个“RFC 伙伴”制度，明确指派初级工程师去评审，并且必须至少提一个问题（消除他们对“该不该留言”的顾虑）。改进后的流程把决策时间从两周缩短到三天，同时通过更多元的 input 提升了决策质量。

Leaders also model the collaborative behaviors they want to see in their teams. When leaders acknowledge uncertainty, consider diverse perspectives, and change their minds based on new evidence, they demonstrate the intellectual humility that enables effective team decision making. Ted Lasso popularized the phrase “Be curious, not judgmental,” which is a tad reductive (and also not a quote by Walt Whitman). But it does highlight an approach we like: asking questions about potential decisions, rather than telling people the answers.

领导者还要示范他们希望在团队中看到的协作行为。当领导者承认不确定性、考虑多元视角、并根据新证据改变主意时，他们展现出的是让团队有效决策成为可能的那种智识上的谦逊。Ted Lasso 让“保持好奇，不要评判”这句话流行开来——它有点过于简化（而且也不是 Walt Whitman 的名言）。但它确实凸显了一种我们喜欢的做法：对潜在的决策多问问题，而不是直接把答案告诉别人。

Conclusion: Collaboration Is the Glue

结语：协作是黏合剂

Collaborative technical practices and decision-making processes are the connective tissue that holds together your team, in the face of the chaos around them. It enables you and your team to achieve outcomes and reduce churn or flail. By establishing shared principles, consistent coding practices, structured decision frameworks like RFCs, and inclusive collaboration patterns, teams can navigate complexity and change while maintaining technical quality and velocity.

协作性技术实践与决策流程，是在周围一片混乱中把团队凝聚在一起的结缔组织。它让你和你的团队能够取得成果、减少人员流失和瞎折腾。通过建立共享原则、一致的编码实践、像 RFC 这样结构化的决策框架、以及包容的协作模式，团队能够在驾驭复杂性与变化的同时，维持技术质量和交付速度。

The most successful teams recognize that these practices aren’t bureaucratic overhead but rather investments that pay dividends through reduced rework, faster alignment, preserved institutional knowledge, and more engaged team members. In chaotic environments where priorities shift frequently and information is often incomplete, strong collaborative practices provide stability and direction.

最成功的团队认识到：这些实践不是官僚式的负担，而是会带来回报的投资——回报体现为减少返工、更快对齐、保住组织知识、以及更投入的团队成员。在优先级频繁变动、信息往往不完整的混乱环境里，扎实的协作实践提供了稳定感和方向。

As you develop your collaborative technical practices, remember that the goal isn’t perfect process adherence but merely somewhat better outcomes through thoughtful collaboration. Start with lightweight frameworks, adapt them to your specific context, and continuously refine them based on your team’s experience. With patience and persistence, you’ll build better software alongside a more resilient and capable engineering organization.

在发展你的协作性技术实践时，请记住：目标不是完美地遵守流程，而只是通过深思熟虑的协作取得稍微更好的结果。从轻量框架起步，根据你的具体情境加以改造，并基于团队的经验持续打磨。凭借耐心与坚持，你会在构建更好软件的同时，建立起一支更有韧性、更有能力的工程组织。
